items.q: Who was Eddie Tipton?
items.a: The information security director of the Multi-State Lottery Association, which ran Hot Lotto and other multi-state games, and one of the programmers of its random number generator. He bought the winning ticket for the 29 December 2010 Iowa Hot Lotto draw, a $14.3 million jackpot that was never paid because the claim came through an anonymous Belize trust that withdrew rather than name him.

items.q: How did he rig the draw?
items.a: Forensic examination of a sister generator in Wisconsin found code added after certification that, on 27 May, 23 November and 29 December, if the date fell on a Wednesday or Saturday draw after 8 p.m., replaced the random draw with numbers he could compute. In June 2017 he confessed to installing it around 2005–2006. Prosecutors had earlier argued he used a draw-room visit on 20 November 2010, with the camera recording one second per minute, to install a self-deleting program.

items.q: Which jackpots were involved?
items.a: Colorado, 23 November 2005 ($568,990 share, claimed by his brother Tommy); Wisconsin, 29 December 2007 ($783,257, via a company of Robert Rhodes); Kansas, 2010; Iowa, 29 December 2010 ($14.3 million, forfeited); Oklahoma, 23 November 2011 ($1.2 million). All on 23 November or 29 December.

items.q: What was the sentence?
items.a: Convicted in July 2015 and sentenced to ten years; the convictions were vacated in June 2017 on the statute of limitations; he then pleaded guilty to ongoing criminal conduct and was sentenced on 22 August 2017 to 25 years, the maximum, with about $2.2 million in restitution split among Colorado, Oklahoma, Wisconsin and Kansas. He was paroled in July 2022 after five years.

items.q: Could this happen to a provably fair game?
items.a: Not by this route. The operator commits to its seed with a published hash before the bet, the player supplies their own seed afterwards, and the result is a function of both, so an insider who wrote the code and holds the server seed still cannot pick the outcome. What remains possible is a server that does not honour its commitment, which is why the hash is published first and the player’s seed is theirs to set.

items.q: What was Hamster Kombat?
items.a: A Telegram mini-app launched in March 2024 in which players tapped a cartoon hamster to accumulate in-game coins, with a promised token airdrop. The makers announced 300 million players on 30 July 2024, the day they published a whitepaper allocating 60% of the HMSTR token to players.

items.q: What happened at the airdrop?
items.a: Claims opened on 26 September 2024 and the token listed on Binance, HashKey, OKX, Bybit, KuCoin and others the same day. 131 million accounts qualified and about 2.3 million were banned for cheating. The price fell about 30% in the first 24 hours, from $0.012 to $0.0087, and reached $0.0025 by 1 November 2024.

items.q: How much did a player get?
items.a: On average about 458 tokens: 60 billion tokens divided by 131 million qualified accounts, a calculation for this article. That was about $5 at the listing price and $1.15 at the November low; many players reported $10 or less. The actual formula weighted coin balances, referrals and card purchases, so most received less than the average.

items.q: How far did the player count fall?
items.a: Reading the mini-app’s own monthly counter: over 100 million in late September 2024 to under 44 million by early November (Decrypt), 40.9 million (ForkLog, 4 November) and 38 million (BitPinas, 6 November). Against the 300 million summer figure that is a fall of about 86% in six weeks.

items.q: Was it a scam?
items.a: Nothing in the public record says so: the token was delivered as the whitepaper described, exchanges listed it, and the bans were for cheating. The collapse is the arithmetic of a fixed pool divided among a growing number of players, paid at a price set on the day 131 million recipients could sell, in a game whose payout was decided after the play rather than before it.

items.q: How much did Don Johnson win, and where?
items.a: About $15 million across three Atlantic City casinos between December 2010 and April 2011: $4.23 million at Caesars in December, roughly $5 million at the Borgata over five months, and $5.8 million at the Tropicana in a single 12-hour session in April 2011, betting $100,000 a hand.

items.q: Was he counting cards?
items.a: No. He was under constant surveillance at $100,000 a hand and the casinos ruled it out; card counting leaves a recognisable betting pattern he did not show. The Tropicana’s CEO described him as a player who makes every decision correctly, which by itself leaves the house a small edge.

items.q: What exactly did he negotiate?
items.a: A trip-to-trip 20% rebate on losses once they passed $500,000, a $100,000 maximum bet with $1 million of his own front money, a hand-shuffled six-deck shoe, the dealer standing on soft 17, and the right to split and double on up to four hands. By his figuring the rules cut the house edge to about 0.25%.

items.q: Why does a 20% rebate beat a 0.25% edge?
items.a: Because the rebate pays only on losses and he controlled when a loss stopped. Quitting at −$500,000 and paying $400,000, while playing on when ahead, makes each attempt worth about +$80,000 to +$90,000 in a fair-game approximation; the 0.25% edge costs about $250 per $100,000 hand, far too little to reverse that. The rebate is an option on variance, and large bets at a small edge maximise variance for minimum drag.

items.q: What happened afterwards?
items.a: The Tropicana’s April 2011 table-game win fell 54.4% year-on-year in the state filings, its president was replaced within weeks, and all three casinos withdrew the terms; Caesars effectively barred him. The Tropicana continued to deal to him with modified discounts, and he says he won a further $2 million there in October 2011 without a rebate.

items.q: What did Jontay Porter do?

items.q: Why are “under” bets the problem?
items.a: An over needs minutes, the ball and made shots; an under needs only that the player stops. A bench player can make every under on his card certain by leaving early at no visible cost, which turns a parlay priced at about 13 to 1 into a near-sure payout.

items.a: $80,000 to win $1.1 million, about 13.75 to 1, consistent with four legs at −110 (1.909⁴ ≈ 13.3). The sportsbook froze it as suspicious and it was never paid.

items.a: That a losing game is survivable only while the stakes are bounded by what you have. Credit from the bookmaker and access to someone else’s account removed the bound, which is how a bad habit became a $40 million hole and a federal case.

items.q: Who is Mohan Srivastava?
items.a: A geological statistician based in Toronto, co-author of a standard textbook on applied geostatistics, who in 2003 found that an Ontario tic-tac-toe scratch ticket could be read before scratching. His story was told by Jonah Lehrer in Wired in 2011.

items.q: What is the singleton method for scratch tickets?
items.a: On tickets that print numbers on their face, count how often each visible number appears. Numbers appearing exactly once — singletons — were, on the flawed 2003 game, almost always the hidden numbers under the latex. Three singletons in a line on one board marked a winner about 90% of the time.

items.q: How much could he have made?
items.a: By his own estimate about $600 a day, at roughly 45 seconds per ticket, with most wins being small prizes. He judged that below his consulting income and reported the flaw instead.

items.q: What did the Ontario lottery do?
items.a: After he mailed 20 unscratched tickets sorted into predicted winners and losers, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation pulled the tic-tac-toe game from retailers within days and described the problem as a design flaw in that game.

The edge is paid per bet, so the more bets the session takes, the lower the chance. At a 2.6–2.8% edge the $1-a-bet chance falls below 1%.

items.q: Is it better to bet big or small to double my money?
items.a: To reach a target, bigger: one bet at 49.995% beats any sequence of smaller bets at the same edge, because every extra bet pays the house again. Smaller bets buy time at the table, not a better chance of the target.

items.q: Do long-shot bets give a better chance of doubling?
items.a: At small stakes, yes. On dice at $1 a bet from $100, a 1-in-100 target at ×100 doubles you 41% of the time against 11% for the 50% target, because it settles in far fewer bets. At $10 a bet the order reverses. The average return is 99% either way.

items.q: How many bets does a session take?
items.a: On dice at 50% with $100: one bet all in, about 100 bets at $10, about 7,600 at $1 and about 19,000 at 50 cents before the bankroll reaches $200 or can no longer cover a bet.

items.q: Which game gives the best chance of doubling?
items.a: The lowest edge at the stake you intend to use: our 1% games (dice, limbo) ahead of Koban Flip at 2%, Chinchiro at 2.6% and Sic Bo Big/Small at 2.8%. At $1 a bet the gap is one chance in nine against one in 240.

items.q: What is the house edge in Chinchiro?
items.a: 2.616% on this table: the return is 97.38% with no commission and whole-number payouts. It comes from the dealer rolling first (specials end the round before you roll), ties going to the dealer, and a dealer no-hand being a push instead of a player win.

items.q: What are the odds of each hand in Chinchiro?
items.a: Per throw: point 41.67%, no hand 50%, shigoro 2.78%, hifumi 2.78%, arashi 2.31%, pinzoro 0.46%. With up to three throws a side ends with a point 72.9%, no hand 12.5%, shigoro or hifumi 4.86%, arashi 4.05%, pinzoro 0.81%.

items.q: How often do I lose before I roll?
items.a: 9.72% of rounds, when the dealer makes pinzoro, arashi or shigoro. The dealer makes hifumi 4.86% of the time (you win ×3 without rolling) and no hand 12.5% (push). You roll in the remaining 72.9%.

items.q: Why does the dealer’s no-hand push instead of losing?
items.a: Because with the street rule the game pays the player 109.88%. Making the dealer’s 12.5% of no-hands a push removes exactly 12.5 points and leaves a 2.62% house edge. It is the one rule here that differs from the traditional game.

items.q: Is there any strategy in Chinchiro?
items.a: No. You do not choose when to roll or stop, and there are no side bets; the only choice is the stake, and the price is 2.616% per unit regardless. Every round is a fresh seed pair, so previous results change nothing.

items.q: What is the house edge in Mines?
items.a: 1% at the top of the table and up to 2.5% at the bottom. Every multiplier is the fair odds floored to two decimals, times 0.99, floored again; the floors cost almost nothing on large multipliers and a point or more on small ones. The worst setting, one mine at two picks (or two mines at one), returns 97.52%.

items.q: Does the house edge grow if I keep picking tiles?
items.a: No. Each rung is priced as the fair odds of the whole run minus 1%, so the return is about 99% wherever you cash out — it rises slightly as you go deeper, because the floors matter less on bigger multipliers. This is unlike a streak game such as RPS, where each extra win compounds the edge.

items.q: Which tiles are safest in Mines?
items.a: None. The mines are placed by a uniform shuffle from the round’s seed pair before your first click, so every closed tile has the same chance of hiding one: mines ÷ tiles still closed. Corners, edges and patterns change nothing.

items.q: What are the odds of clearing the board?
items.a: C(25 − m, k) ÷ C(25, k) with all safe tiles opened: 1 in 25 with one mine, 1 in 2,300 with three (×2,277), 1 in 53,130 with five (×52,598.70), 1 in 3,268,760 with ten. Each pays exactly 99% of fair, subject to the maximum profit per round.

items.q: How many mines should I choose?
items.a: The mine count changes the shape of the ride, not its price: more mines mean fewer, bigger steps. Settings whose multipliers are small — few mines and few picks — lose the most to the two-decimal floors; every rung that pays ×2.20 or more returns 98.5% or better.

items.q: What are the odds of winning rock paper scissors against a casino dealer?
items.a: Here the dealer’s hand is a uniform random draw, so any throw wins, draws and loses one time in three. Because a draw replays, the round is decided 50/50.

items.q: What is the house edge on RPS?
items.a: 1.5% per win: a win pays ×1.97 and happens half the time once draws are taken out, so each win returns 98.5%. Counting draws as rounds that returned the stake gives 1% per throw — the same game described differently.

items.q: Should I cash out after one win or keep going?
items.a: Each extra win is a new even-money bet of your whole running multiplier at 98.5%, so the edge compounds: cashing after 2 wins returns 97.0%, after 5 wins 92.7%, after 10 wins 86.0%. Banking the first win and starting again is the cheapest way to play.

items.q: Is there a best throw in rock paper scissors here?
items.a: No. The dealer’s hand comes from the seed pair and does not depend on your throw or on previous rounds, so every throw has the same one-in-three chances.

items.q: What does a draw do?
items.a: Nothing is paid and nothing is lost; you throw again. You cannot cash out on a draw before your first win.

items.q: What is the RTP of the Tairyō slot?
items.a: About 96.2–96.4%: 29.41% exactly from base-game line wins, plus free spins that trigger once in 385.8 spins and pay about ×258 on average. The engine’s comment records a simulated 95.2%, about a point lower.

items.q: How often do Tairyō free spins trigger?
items.a: On 0.2592% of spins, one in 385.8. It needs a scatter on each of reels 2, 3 and 4, shown 18%, 12% and 12% of the time. Four or five scatters cannot occur.

items.q: How much do Tairyō free spins pay?
items.a: About ×258 the bet on average, but ×56 in the middle case. About 21% of rounds pay under ×10, 4.6% pay ×1,000 or more and 0.2% reach the ×2,100 cap.

items.q: Is buying the Tairyō bonus worth it?
items.a: It returns about 95.5% (regular, 270×) or 95.3% (super, 720×), slightly less than the roughly 96.2% the game returns when the round is triggered by spinning. Two buys in three pay back less than their price.

items.q: Why does Tairyō lose so fast between features?
items.a: The base game returns 29.41% on its own. Two-thirds of the return sits in the free-spin round, so a 100-spin session without the feature — 77% of them — keeps about 29% of its stakes.

items.q: What does the ×10 multiplier apply to?
items.a: Only to the fish values the wilds collect, from the ninth collected wild onward. Line wins in free spins are paid at face value.

items.q: What are the odds of a Banker streak in baccarat?
items.a: With ties ignored, each decided hand is Banker 50.68% of the time on an eight-deck shoe, so a Banker run that has started reaches k hands with probability 0.5068^(k−1). In one 90-round road, a Banker run of 6 or more appears 49.5% of the time and 10 or more 4.0%.

items.q: How often does a 20-hand baccarat streak happen?
items.a: On one table dealing a round every 12 seconds, a Banker run of 20 or more happens about once in 249 days. Across Dragon Road’s 2,000 tables it happens about 8 times a day, and a Player run of 20 or more about 5 times.

items.q: Does a long streak change the odds of the next hand?
items.a: No. Every Dragon Road hand is dealt from a fresh eight-deck shoe, so the next hand is Banker 45.86%, Player 44.62%, Tie 9.52% whatever the road shows.

items.q: Why does the Dragon Road lobby always show long streaks?
items.a: It lists the 24 longest current streaks out of 2,000 tables and pauses dealing on those tables so the road you see is the road you play. The streaks are selected, not hot.

items.q: What is the house edge in Dragon Road?
Do ties break a streak?
items.a: No. A tie leaves the streak unchanged, and Banker and Player bets are returned on a tie.

items.q: What is the RTP of the Hanabi slot?
items.a: Exactly 95.81%, computed from the symbol weights: 66.17% from line wins, 2.87% from scatter pays and 26.77% from the free-spin feature. The engine header’s 96.1% was a simulation estimate about three-tenths of a point too high.

items.q: How often do Hanabi free spins trigger?

items.q: How much are Hanabi free spins worth?

items.q: Which Hanabi symbol pays the most over time?
items.a: 麺 Yakisoba, at 15.57% of the return, followed by 鈴 Suzu at 12.46%. The two cheapest symbols land most often; the ×40 金魚 contributes 5.99%.

items.q: How often does a spin pay?

items.q: Can a Hanabi round hit the ×2,000 cap?
items.a: In principle; in two million replayed features the largest paid ×513.8, so the cap has no measurable effect on the return.

items.q: What are the real odds in a dice game that rolls 0 to 100?
items.a: Here the roll is one of 9,999 results from 0.01 to 99.99. Roll under T wins on 100 × T − 1 of them, so roll under 50 is 49.995%, roll under 10 is 9.991% and roll under 2 is 1.990%.

items.q: What is the house edge on dice?
items.a: The stated edge is 1%, but the true return depends on the target: from 99.00% at a target of 90 to 98.03% at 97.06. Averaged over every slider setting from 2.00 to 98.00 it is 98.72%, an effective edge of 1.28%.

items.q: Why does my dice multiplier look rounded down?
items.a: The engine pays 0.99 ÷ win chance floored to two decimals. At an 80% target that is 1.2375, paid as ×1.23, which returns 98.40% instead of 99%.

items.q: What is the best target to pick in dice?
items.a: Any target where 0.99 ÷ chance divides exactly, such as 50 (×1.98), 25 (×3.96), 90 (×1.10) or 66 (×1.50). Typing the multiplier instead of the percentage finds one automatically. No target returns more than 99%.

items.q: What happens if the dice roll lands exactly on my target?
items.a: It loses. Under wins only below the target and Over only above it, so a roll of exactly 50.00 loses both Under 50 and Over 50. It happens once in 9,999 rolls.

items.q: Can I verify a dice roll?
items.a: Yes. HMAC-SHA256 of “clientSeed-nonce-0” keyed by the revealed server seed; the first 13 hex digits over 2⁵² give u, and (floor(u × 9,999) + 1) ÷ 100 is the result.

items.q: What are the odds of getting a bingo line?
items.a: On this 38-of-75 solo card, 37.18% of rounds complete at least one line: 28.60% exactly one, 7.06% two, 1.29% three, 0.20% four, 0.029% five, 0.0041% six, and seven or more once in 155,000.

items.q: What is the house edge in solo bingo?
items.a: Exactly 3.34%: the return is 96.66% of the stake, computed over every possible mark pattern rather than simulated. The design notes’ simulated 96.5% was an estimate of this number.

items.q: Why is the free centre worth a whole ball?
items.a: A line through the centre needs four drawn numbers instead of five, so it completes 6.07% of the time against 2.91% — about twice as often. Four of the twelve lines pass through it.

items.q: Can you complete 11 lines?
items.a: No. Every cell is on one row and one column, so any unmarked number breaks at least two lines at once; you can lose lines two at a time but never exactly one, and the count jumps from ten (one unmarked number off the diagonals) to twelve. All twelve happens once in 2.67 billion cards.

items.q: How many numbers on the card usually get marked?
items.a: On average 12.16 of the 24. Twelve marks exactly is the single most likely outcome (19.5%); twenty or more happens once in about 10,500 rounds.

items.q: Which payout gives most of the return?
items.a: The single line at ×1.5, which pays on 28.6% of rounds and accounts for 42.9% of the 96.66% return. One and two lines together are 71% of it; everything from ×100 up is 4%.

items.q: Can I verify a bingo round?
items.a: Yes. One HMAC-SHA256 per cursor keyed by the revealed server seed over “clientSeed-nonce-cursor”: cursors 0–24 deal the card, 25–62 draw the balls, and the verifier’s bingo command reproduces both and the line count.

items.q: What are the odds of reaching the top in Pagoda?
items.a: Nine floors in a row: 7.5% on Easy (1 in 13.3), 2.6% on Medium (1 in 38.4) and 0.2% on Hard (1 in 512). Each floor is cleared with probability (tiles − 1) ÷ tiles and the floors are independent.

items.q: What is the house edge in Pagoda?
items.a: Target 1% at every cash-out point. The engine floors each multiplier to cents, so the actual return is exactly 99.00% on Hard and on Easy floors one and two, and between 98.67% and 98.99% on the other Easy and Medium rungs.

items.q: Which difficulty is the best value?
items.a: Hard, marginally: all nine of its rungs return exactly 99.00% because 0.99 × 2ᵏ is a whole number of cents. Easy and Medium lose up to a third of a cent per stake to flooring on some rungs. The difference is at most 0.33% of the stake; the difference in swing between the modes is far larger.

items.q: What does the Pagoda ladder pay?
Does it matter which tile I pick?
items.a: No. The trap on every floor is fixed by the seed pair and nonce before the round starts, and every tile is equally likely to be it, so any habit — always left, always the same column — has the same (tiles − 1) in tiles chance.

items.q: Is it better to cash out early or climb?
items.a: Neither in expectation: every rung costs about 1%. Cashing out early collects that 1% in small frequent losses with a swing near one stake per round; climbing collects it in rare large payouts with a swing of up to 22 stakes per round on Hard.

items.q: Can I verify a Pagoda round?
items.a: Yes. One HMAC-SHA256 per floor keyed by the revealed server seed over “clientSeed-nonce-floor”, first 8 bytes ÷ 2⁶⁴, times the tile count and floored, gives each trap; the verifier’s pagoda command reproduces the layout and the ladder.

items.q: What are the odds of hitting a single number in roulette?
items.a: 1 in 37 per spin on this single-zero wheel, 2.70%. The number lands at least once in 37 spins 63.7% of the time and in 100 spins 93.5% of the time; the median wait is 26 spins and the mean is 37.

items.q: How many spins does it take for a number to come up?
items.a: On average 37, but half of all waits are 26 spins or fewer and a few are very long: no hit in 100 spins happens 6.5% of the time, no hit in 200 spins 0.4%.

items.q: What are the odds of red coming up 10 times in a row?
items.a: (18 ÷ 37)¹⁰ = 0.074%, about 1 in 1,350. A losing run of ten on an even-money bet, which includes zero, is 0.128%, about 1 in 780. Neither changes the next spin, which is 18 ÷ 37 red regardless.

items.q: How often does zero come up in roulette?
items.a: Once in 37 spins on average. Zero appears at least once in 37 spins 63.7% of the time and in 74 spins 86.8%; it is absent from a full 37-spin cycle more than a third of the time.

items.q: Is a straight-up bet worse than red?
items.a: Not in price: both return 97.30% on this wheel. A straight-up bet is far more volatile — a standard deviation of 5.84 stakes a spin against 1.00 for red — so it produces long dry runs and occasional ×36 wins rather than a steady drift.

items.q: Can I verify a roulette spin?
items.a: Yes. HMAC-SHA256 of “clientSeed-nonce-0” keyed by the revealed server seed, first eight bytes as a fraction of 2⁶⁴, times 37 and floored, gives the pocket; the verifier’s roulette command does it in one step.

items.q: What are the odds on the wheel game?
items.a: On this engine’s 48-slot wheel: 25 slots pay nothing (52.08%), 13 pay ×1.5 (27.08%), 7 pay ×2 (14.58%), 2 pay ×3 (4.17%) and 1 pays ×8 (2.08%). Any win lands 23 times in 48, 47.92%.

items.q: What is the house edge on the wheel?
items.a: 1.04%. The multipliers sum to 47.5 across 48 slots, so a spin returns 47.5 ÷ 48 = 98.96% of the stake on average. That is in the same band as limbo and crash and well under roulette or the colour wheel.

items.q: How often does the ×8 hit?
items.a: Once in 48 spins on average, a median of once every 33. The chance of no ×8 in 48 spins is 36%, and in 100 spins 12%. The ×8 carries a sixth of the wheel’s return; a wheel without it would return 82.3%.

items.q: Why does the wheel lose more than half the time if the edge is only 1%?
items.a: Because the wins are paid nearly in full. 25 of 48 slots pay zero, but the 23 paying slots are priced so that their multipliers sum to 47.5. A low edge and a low win rate are different properties: the wheel has a low edge and a win rate under one half.

items.q: How many wheel spins are there in an hour?
items.a: About 183. A round is a 10-second betting window, a 0.7-second lock and a 9-second spin, roughly 19.7 seconds. A flat one-unit stake every spin costs about 1.9 units an hour on average, with a swing of about 19 units.

items.q: Can I verify a wheel spin?
items.a: Yes. Each round reveals its chain link; HMAC-SHA256 of the public salt keyed by that link, first seven bytes divided by 2⁵⁶, times 48 and floored, gives the slot. Read the multiplier off the published 48-slot layout, and check that SHA-256 of the link equals the previous round’s link.

items.q: What are the odds of green in Double?
items.a: 1 in 15, or 6.67% a round, because the wheel has one green tile among fifteen. Green pays ×14 (a profit of thirteen stakes). The average wait between greens is 15 rounds and the median is 11; the chance of no green in 30 rounds is 12.6%.

items.q: What is the house edge in Double?
items.a: 6.67% on every colour. Red and black win 7 in 15 and pay ×2 (return 93.33%); green wins 1 in 15 and pays ×14 (return 93.33%). The wheel is built so that tiles × multiplier = 14 for each colour, and 14 ÷ 15 is the return of any bet or combination of bets.

items.q: Is betting red and black at the same time a good strategy?
items.a: It lowers the swing, not the price. Red plus black returns the pair 14 times in 15 and loses both stakes on green, which is still a 93.33% return — a 6.67% edge on twice the money. No combination of colours returns more than 14 ÷ 15.

items.q: Is green in Double a bad bet?
items.a: No worse than red or black in expectation: all three return 93.33%. Green is far more volatile — a standard deviation of 3.49 stakes a round against 1.00 for red — so it pays rarely and big rather than often and small. Choose it for the variance, not the value.

items.q: How many rounds of Double are there in an hour?
items.a: About 192. A round is a 12-second betting window, a 0.7-second lock and a 6-second result phase, roughly 18.7 seconds in all. A flat one-unit bet every round costs about 12.8 units an hour on average at the 6.67% edge.

items.q: Can I verify a Double spin?
items.a: Yes. Each round reveals its chain link; HMAC-SHA256 of the public salt keyed by that link, first seven bytes divided by 2⁵⁶, times 15 and floored, gives the slot (0 green, 1–7 red, 8–14 black). SHA-256 of the link must equal the previous round’s link, back to the published commit hash.

items.q: What are the odds of winning at ×2 in crash?
items.a: 49.50% on this engine. A target pays only when the round busts strictly above it, and the chance the bust point is at least 201 hundredths is 99 ÷ 200. The curve reaches ×2.00 slightly more often, 49.75%; the difference is the one round in 402 that busts on exactly ×2.00.

items.q: What is the house edge in crash?
items.a: 1.00% at every cash-out target, manual or auto. The win chance is 99 ÷ target in hundredths and the payout is the target, so every bet returns 99.00% of the stake on average — the same price as limbo on this engine.

items.q: How often does crash bust at 1.00?
items.a: Exactly 1% of rounds, one in a hundred. The bust point is floor((100 − u) ÷ (1 − u)) hundredths, which is 100 whenever u is below 1 ÷ 100. No target, not even ×1.01, is paid on those rounds.

items.q: What is the best cash-out multiplier for crash?
items.a: None in expectation: every target costs 1% per unit staked. Low targets pay small amounts often and keep the swing near one stake; high targets pay rarely and swing by tens of stakes. ×1.98 is the exact 50/50 point and the median bust.

items.q: How long does a crash round last?
items.a: The multiplier doubles every ten seconds, so ×2 arrives at 10.0 s, ×10 at 33.2 s, ×100 at 66.4 s and the ×10,000 cap at 132.9 s. The median round busts just under ten seconds in; the average round lasts 14.3 seconds.

items.q: Can a ×10,000 auto target ever pay?
items.a: No. ×10,000.00 is the bust cap, and a target must be strictly below the bust to pay, so the highest target that can ever be paid is ×9,999.99, once in 10,101 rounds.

items.q: Is crash cheaper than limbo for short rides?
items.a: Not on this engine. An earlier article priced crash from the chance the curve reaches a multiplier and found 99.99% at ×1.01; under the strict settlement the chance that counts is one hundredth lower, and the return is exactly 99.00% at every target, as in limbo.

items.q: What are the odds of winning in limbo?
items.a: On this engine, 99 divided by your target: 49.50% at ×2, 9.90% at ×10, 0.99% at ×100 and 0.0099% (one in 10,101) at the ×10,000 cap. The formula is exact because the drawn number is floor(99 ÷ (1 − u)) and the target is a whole number of hundredths.

items.q: What is the house edge in limbo?
items.a: 1.00% at every target. The win chance is 99 ÷ target and the payout is the target, so every bet returns 99.00% of the stake on average. No target multiplier is better value than another; a higher target only makes the results swing more.

items.q: What is the best target multiplier for limbo?
items.a: There is no better target in expectation — all of them cost 1% per unit staked. Low targets like ×1.10 or ×1.50 pay small amounts often; high targets pay rarely and big. Choose by how much variance you want, not by value, and remember that at ×100 you have a 37% chance of no win at all in 100 rounds.

items.q: How often does limbo crash at 1.00?
items.a: 1.98% of rounds, about one in fifty. The formula starts at 0.99 ÷ (1 − u), so the lowest 1.98% of draws produce a number below ×1.01, and no target can win on those rounds.

items.q: Is ×2 in limbo a 50/50 bet?
items.a: Not quite: 49.50%. The exact 50% point is ×1.98, which is the median outcome. The half-point gap between ×1.98 and ×2.00 is the house edge at that target.

items.q: Does the rounding in the formula cost the player anything?
items.a: No. The floor in floor(99 ÷ (1 − u)) only decides the two decimals shown; because targets are whole hundredths, floor(x) ≥ T exactly when x ≥ T, so the win chance is 99 ÷ target without any rounding loss. The demo payout is floored to the cent, which matters only on small odd stakes.

items.q: What are the odds of hitting all 10 numbers in keno?
items.a: One in 847,660,528 on a 40-number board with 10 balls drawn — that is C(40, 10), the number of distinct draws, and exactly one of them matches a ten-pick ticket. On this engine that cell pays ×1,000 on Low, Medium and High and ×100 on Classic.

items.q: What are the odds of hitting 5 out of 5 in keno?
items.a: One in 2,611 (0.038%). Four of five hits happens 0.96% of the time and three of five 7.93%. The engine pays five for five at ×36 on Classic, ×300 on Low, ×390 on Medium and ×450 on High.

items.q: How many numbers should I pick in keno?
items.a: The return is within half a point across every pick count and level (98.65% to 99.07%), so no pick count is better value. More picks means more hits on average — exactly one quarter of the marks — but the table demands more hits before it pays. Fewer picks means a simpler ticket that either hits or does not.

items.q: How many numbers will I hit on average?
items.a: A quarter of the numbers you mark, because 10 of the 40 are drawn. Ten picks average 2.5 hits and land on exactly two 31.07% of the time; four picks average one hit. Missing everything runs from 75.00% with one pick down to 3.54% with ten.

items.q: Does picking the same numbers every game improve my odds?
items.a: No. Every ten-ball draw is equally likely and independent of the last, so no set of numbers is due or cold. The odds of any hit count depend only on how many numbers you mark, and those odds are the chart in this article.

items.q: Is the ×1,000 keno prize worth chasing?
items.a: It is worth 0.00012% of the stake on a ten-pick ticket — ×1,000 multiplied by a one-in-847,660,528 chance. Almost all of the ticket’s 99% return is paid on ordinary hit counts, and on High nothing below four hits pays at all.

items.q: What did Uston v. Resorts International decide?
items.a: On 5 May 1982 the New Jersey Supreme Court held that an Atlantic City casino could not exclude Kenneth Uston for card counting. The Casino Control Act gives the Casino Control Commission exclusive authority over the rules of licensed games, Uston had broken none of them, and only the Commission could change them. The court left open whether the Commission itself could adopt a rule excluding counters.

items.q: Why could Nevada casinos bar Uston but New Jersey casinos could not?
items.a: Uston’s Nevada suits, decided in 1977 and 1978, failed because a private casino excluding a player is not the state acting, and Nevada law imposes no duty to admit a suspected counter. New Jersey’s Casino Control Act places every rule of play under the Commission, so a casino cannot add a private rule of its own. New Jersey’s position remains a minority rule in the United States.

items.q: How did the Casino Control Commission respond to the ruling?
items.a: With rule changes rather than a ban. Amendments published in June 1982 and adopted in August 1982 let casinos shuffle after any round, use the Bart Carter shuffle, install continuous-shuffling shoes and use more decks. In 1991 a further rule let a casino change a table’s minimum and maximum wager at any time without notifying the Commission.

items.q: Is card counting illegal?
items.a: No. Counting with your own memory is not a crime anywhere in the United States. What differs is whether a casino may refuse to deal to you for it: in New Jersey it may not, but it may shuffle at will and adjust limits; in Nevada and most other states it may simply ask you to leave. Devices that count for you are a separate and criminal matter in many places.

items.q: Can you count cards in online blackjack?
items.a: Not on an infinite-shoe game such as this site’s. Each card is floor(u × 52) where u comes from HMAC-SHA256 of the committed server seed over clientSeed-nonce-cursor, so every card is an independent draw with replacement. Nothing depletes, so there is nothing to count and no countermeasure to apply. Live-dealer games with a physical shoe are the exception, which is why they shuffle early.

items.q: What are the odds in the Hi-Lo card game?
items.a: Each card is drawn uniformly from thirteen ranks. On a card of rank r, “Higher or same” wins (14 − r) times in 13 and “Lower or same” wins r times in 13 — the current rank pays on both sides. On an Ace or a King one button becomes “Same”, which wins 1 time in 13. Suits are irrelevant to settlement.

items.q: What is the house edge in Hi-Lo?
items.a: At the 1% setting, between 1.0000% and 1.0038% on every button, for one call or for a long run. Since version 3 the engine multiplies exact step odds, applies the return once and floors once at four decimals, so no button and no ladder length is materially cheaper than another.

items.q: Why does the Hi-Lo button show ×1.07 and not ×1.08?
items.a: The fair price of a 92.31% call is 13 ÷ 12 = 1.0833. On the first correct call of a run the 1% return is applied in the same move, and the button shows that figure floored to two decimals, ×1.07; the ticket actually pays ×1.0725. From the second call onwards the same button reads ×1.08 because the return has already been taken.

items.q: Is it better to call the likely side or the long shot in Hi-Lo?
items.a: Neither is cheaper: the difference between always taking the cheaper side and always taking the more likely side is half a thousandth of a point of house edge. The choice sets how often you win and how much, not what you pay.

items.q: Does a longer Hi-Lo run pay better than cashing out early?
items.a: It pays the same 1% edge. Ten straight ×1.08 calls reach ×2.2042 with a 44.91% chance at a 1.0012% edge; sixty reach ×120.60 with a 0.82% chance at 1.0000%. Longer runs are rarer, not dearer.

items.q: Does skipping a card in Hi-Lo help?
items.a: Skipping costs nothing and risks nothing — a new card is dealt, the multiplier and pot stand — and you can do it up to 52 times in a run. But the replacement card comes from the same thirteen ranks and every button costs the same 1%, so a skip only changes the shape of the next call, not its price.

items.q: What did Hi-Lo version 3 change?
items.a: Two things. The first card of a real-money run is now dealt by the server from the ticket’s seed stream instead of by the client, and the run multiplier is the exact product of step odds times the return, floored once at four decimals — replacing the older rule that floored every step and the total to two decimals and cost up to 2.15% on a single call.

items.q: What is the house edge on Banker in baccarat?
items.a: On this engine’s deal, with Banker paying 0.95 to 1, the house edge is 1.06% of the amount staked (1.18% if ties are excluded). On a standard eight-deck shoe the same rules give 1.058%.

items.q: Is it better to bet Banker or Player?
items.a: Banker costs less: 1.06% against 1.23% on Player, even after the 5% commission. Banker wins 45.84% of deals and Player 44.61%, because Banker’s drawing rule can react to Player’s third card.

items.q: Why does the Banker bet charge a commission?
items.a: Without it Banker would favour the player by 1.23%. Any commission above 2.68% turns it back into a house bet; the 5% commission leaves a 1.06% edge.

items.q: What are the odds of a tie in baccarat?
items.a: A tie comes up in 9.54% of deals, about once in 10.48. The Tie bet pays 8 to 1 here, which gives it a 14.12% house edge — the most expensive main bet on the table.

items.q: Are the pair side bets worth it?
items.a: They cost more than Banker or Player. A pair comes up 1 time in 13 on the engine’s demo deal and pays 11 to 1, an edge of 7.69%. On an eight-deck shoe the chance drops to 31 in 415 and the edge rises to 10.36%.

items.q: Does the martingale strategy work in roulette?
items.a: It wins small amounts often and loses large amounts rarely, and the average is always a loss. On a single-zero wheel every martingale, at any depth, loses exactly 2.70% of the total amount staked. With 10 doublings a series busts once in about 784 series and loses 0.31 units on average.

items.q: How much bankroll does the martingale need?
items.a: 2ⁿ − 1 units to survive n bets. Ten bets need 1,023 units, seventeen need 131,071. On this engine’s demo table (minimum 1, maximum 100,000) seventeen bets is the most the limit allows.

items.q: How likely is a losing streak of 10 in roulette?
items.a: On an even-money bet on a single-zero wheel, a run of at least 10 losses appears somewhere in 100 spins 5.6% of the time and somewhere in 1,000 spins 46.2% of the time. The next spin after such a run still wins 18 times in 37.

items.q: If a martingale session usually ends in profit, how can it lose on average?
items.a: Because the losing sessions are much larger. With 1,023 units and a +100 target, 88.0% of sessions reach the target, but the other 12.0% lose most of the bankroll, and the expected result of a session is −28.7 units.

items.q: Is there a betting system that beats the house edge?
items.a: No system that only changes stake sizes can. Each spin is independent and returns 36/37 of its stake on average, so any sequence of stakes returns 36/37 of their total. Stake sizing changes the variance and the risk of ruin, not the edge.

items.q: What is the basic strategy for blackjack when the dealer stands on soft 17?
items.a: On this engine (infinite shoe, S17, 3:2, double after split, one split, peek): stand on hard 17+, stand on 13–16 against 2–6 and hit against 7+, stand on 12 against 4–6, double 11 against 2–10, double 10 against 2–9, double 9 against 3–6, always split aces and eights, never split fives or tens. The full chart, including soft hands and pairs, is above.

items.q: Should you hit or stand on 16 against a dealer 10?
items.a: Hit, but it barely matters. On this infinite shoe hitting loses 0.5398 of a bet on average and standing loses 0.5404, a difference of 0.0006. It is the closest call on the chart.

items.q: Should you split tens against a dealer 5 or 6?
items.a: No. Against a 6, a pair of tens is worth +0.704 of a bet standing and +0.576 split. Splitting gives up about 0.128 of a bet every time, the most expensive common mistake on the chart.

items.q: What is the house edge in blackjack with perfect basic strategy?
items.a: For this engine’s rules the exact return is 99.43%, a house edge of 0.57%, computed for this article; the engine header states it as about 99.5%. Mimicking the dealer returns about 94.3%.

items.q: Why does 11 hit against an ace instead of doubling?
items.a: Because the dealer stands on soft 17 and has already been checked for blackjack. Hitting 11 against an ace is worth +0.143 of a bet and doubling +0.109. Against a dealer who hits soft 17 the double becomes correct.

items.q: Should I keep a low pair or two high cards in video poker?
items.a: Keep the low pair. On this engine’s 8/5 Jacks or Better table a pair of sixes next to a king and a queen returns 0.81 units on average; keeping the king and queen returns 0.49. The pair reaches trips, two pair and full houses often enough to beat the honours’ occasional ×1 save.

items.q: Should I break a pair of jacks for a four-card flush?
items.a: No. The pair returns 1.53 units; drawing at the four-flush returns 1.06. The flush arrives in 9 of 47 draws and ×5 does not cover the 38 misses.

items.q: Should I break a made flush for three to the royal?
items.a: No. The flush is worth 5.00 units in hand; three to the royal returns 1.31 on the draw. Four to the royal is different: it returns 19.45, which beats a made straight (4.00) but not a made straight flush (50).

items.q: Does the 8/5 paytable change the correct holds?
items.a: Not in any of the classic cases. It lowers the value of flush and full-house outcomes slightly, so a few marginal decisions elsewhere shift, but the ranking of every hold in this article is the same as on the 9/6 table. The table changes the price of the game, not the strategy.

items.q: How were these numbers computed?
items.a: By exact enumeration for this article: every combination of replacement cards from the 47 unseen was dealt for each hold, the resulting hand was paid from the engine’s VP_PAYTABLE, and the payouts were averaged. There is no simulation and no rounding beyond the two decimals shown.

items.q: Is gambling legal in Japan?
items.a: Gambling is a crime under Chapter 23 of the Penal Code. It is legal only where a specific statute permits it: the four public races (horse, keirin, auto race, motorboat), the takarakuji lottery, the toto sports lottery, and, since the 2018 integrated-resort law, licensed casino resorts.

items.q: What are the kōei kyōgi?
items.a: The four public races on which betting is permitted by law: horse racing (betting from 1923, JRA from 1954), keirin (1948), auto race (1950) and kyōtei motorboat racing (1951, racing from 1952). Each is run by a public body and its proceeds fund government and designated causes.

items.q: How much do the public races pay back?
items.a: The Horse Racing Act returns 75% of sales to bettors; keirin and motorboat racing sit at about the same rate and auto race at about 70%, all fixed by law. On the house-edge scale a casino uses, that is a 25% edge, against 2.7% for single-zero roulette and 1–3.5% for the originals on this site.

items.q: What is pari-mutuel betting?
items.a: All wagers on a race go into one pool; the operator deducts the share the law allows and the rest is shared among the winning tickets in proportion to their stakes. The operator carries no risk on the result, and the displayed odds are the state of the pool, not a fixed price.

items.q: How big is the market?
items.a: The JRA reported about ¥3.36 trillion in sales for 2024, its fifth consecutive year above ¥3 trillion; secondary estimates put all four public races at roughly ¥8.5 trillion for the year.

items.q: Where do the Journal’s odds figures come from?
items.a: From the game’s derivation or paytable module in the client engine, quoted by file and symbol in a verified block. Returns are computed from those tables, not copied from marketing pages or other sites.

items.q: What does a verified block mean?
items.a: It is a citation naming the engine file and constant the figure was read from, sometimes quoting the source comment. It is not a certification or an audit statement.

items.q: What happens when the engine and a page disagree?
items.a: The engine is treated as the fact, the page is corrected, and the discrepancy is reported to the game’s owners. This process has found a mispriced Plinko cell and a wrong pay-line count in a guide.

items.q: Is the data available for reuse?
items.a: Yes. The tables are published as JSON and CSV at betkyo.com/data/ under a Creative Commons attribution licence, each file naming its source module and article, and mirrored with the derivation scripts and the round verifier on GitHub at github.com/betkyo-open-labs.

items.q: Does verification mean the games have no house edge?
items.a: No. Every game has a published edge, computed in its article. Verification means the numbers and the randomness can be checked, not that the price is zero.

items.q: What is the difference between RTP and house edge?
items.a: They are the same number from two sides. RTP is the share of stakes paid back on average; the house edge is one minus RTP. A 97.3% RTP is a 2.7% house edge.

items.q: What does provably fair actually prove?
items.a: That the house committed to its randomness before you bet, that the revealed seed is the committed one, and that every result follows from the seed pair and round number. It does not prove the game has no house edge.

items.q: What is the difference between a nonce and a cursor?
items.a: The nonce counts rounds across the whole site; the cursor counts random draws inside one round. Together with the seed pair they identify every number the engine produces.

items.q: What is volatility in a casino game?
items.a: How widely results spread around the average, usually the standard deviation of the payout in stakes. Risk levels change volatility while leaving the return almost unchanged.

items.q: What is risk of ruin?
items.a: The probability a bankroll hits zero before a target. It depends on bet size relative to bankroll and on variance; with a negative edge and no stopping rule it is one.

items.q: Why does the withdraw button stay disabled?
items.a: Because one of the checks failed: the amount is not positive, exceeds your balance, or is below the coin’s minimum, or a required field such as the network, tag or six-digit code is missing. The message under the amount says which.

items.q: Where do I see the minimum and the fee?
items.a: In the warning text under the form, for the coin and network you have selected. Both are stored per coin in the coin’s smallest unit and shown converted to normal units.

items.q: Why is there a network selector for some coins?
items.a: Because those coins exist on more than one chain. The request carries the base coin of the network you choose so the transfer goes down the chain your receiving wallet watches.

items.q: What is the tag field?
items.a: A destination tag or memo for coins whose address identifies a shared wallet. It is sent as its own field only for those coins; without it the funds arrive at the address but not at you.

items.q: Does the window check the address?
items.a: Only that it is present. It cannot tell whose address it is, which is why you should copy it from the place that issued it and read more than the first and last characters.

items.q: Who was Tommy Glenn Carmichael?
items.a: A Tulsa television repairman who cheated slot machines from about 1980 to 1996 with home-made devices: the top-bottom joint, the monkey paw and the light wand. He was imprisoned in 1985, arrested again in 1996, pleaded guilty in 2001 and was added to Nevada’s Black Book in 2003.

items.q: How did the light wand work?
items.a: A small bulb on a camera battery, slipped into the payout slot, blinded the optical sensor that counted coins leaving the hopper. The machine had decided a payout correctly but could no longer see how much it had paid, so the hopper kept paying.

items.q: How is that different from the Ronald Harris case?
items.a: Harris altered the decision by putting code into machines that produced jackpots on demand. Carmichael left the decision alone and fooled the delivery. They attacked opposite ends of the machine.

items.q: Why does this not apply to an online game?
items.a: Because there is no delivery to fool. The payout here is the stake times the result’s multiplier, rounded to cents and credited directly; the result is a function of a committed seed. Decision and payout are one computation with no sensor between them.

items.q: What is the Black Book?
items.a: Nevada’s List of Excluded Persons. A person on it may not enter any casino in the state, and a casino that admits them can be penalised.

items.q: What happened at the Ritz casino in 2004?
items.a: Over two nights in March 2004 three players won about £1.3 million at roulette in the Ritz Club, London. Police alleged they used a laser scanner hidden in a phone, linked to a computer, to predict the sector where the ball would land. They were arrested, but in December 2004 no charges were brought and the money was returned.

items.q: Why were they not charged?
items.a: The law then in force, the Gaming Act 1845, addressed fraud and unlawful devices used in the game itself. The scanner measured the spin without touching the ball, the wheel or the dealer, so the police concluded no offence had been committed. The Gambling Act 2005 later widened the definition of cheating.

items.q: How does a laser scanner predict roulette?
items.a: It times the ball and the wheel in the first seconds after release. From those speeds and the wheel’s geometry a computer estimates where the ball will leave the track and which sector of the rotor will be beneath it, and the player bets that sector before betting closes. The target is a sector, not a single number, because of scatter after the ball drops.

items.q: Is sector targeting the same as wheel bias?
items.a: No. Wheel bias exploits a defective wheel and needs thousands of recorded spins to find. Sector targeting exploits a perfectly good wheel by measuring a single spin in progress. Both are observation rather than interference, which is why courts in England and Spain treated them as they did.

items.q: Can an online roulette wheel be predicted this way?
items.a: Not on this site. The pocket is floor(u × 37) where u comes from a hash of the committed server seed, your client seed and the round number. There is no ball in motion and no measurement to take; what you can check instead is that the revealed seed matches the commitment and reproduces every past spin.

items.q: What is the machine zone?
items.a: The absorbed, time-blind state that continuous machine play produces. Natasha Dow Schüll documented it in Addiction by Design (2012) and argued that it is manufactured by machine and floor design rather than brought by the player.

items.q: What are losses disguised as wins?
items.a: Spins on multi-line slots that return less than the total stake but are presented with the sound and light of a win. Research by Dixon and colleagues shows they produce the physiological response of a win and lead players to overestimate how often they won.

items.q: What is time on device?
items.a: The industry’s measure of how long a player stays at a machine. Speed, continuous play, disguised losses, near misses and floor design are levers that extend it.

items.q: Does this site use those levers?
items.a: The floor levers do not exist in a browser, and results are shown as a plain multiplier with no separate win display, so a round below stake reads as a loss. Speed is real, and the pause between rounds has to be the player’s own.

items.q: What is the practical defence?
items.a: Decide the end of the session before it starts, using the settings page limits; keep a clock in view; read the multiplier rather than the animation; and stop on a schedule rather than on a feeling.

items.q: What is the house money effect?
items.a: The tendency to take more risk with money recently won than with money you started with, as if the winnings still belonged to the casino. Thaler and Johnson documented it in 1990.

items.q: What is the break-even effect?
items.a: After a loss, people generally avoid risk but will eagerly take a gamble that could return them exactly to their starting point, even at poor odds. Thaler and Johnson named it alongside the house money effect.

items.q: Why does it happen?
items.a: Mental accounting: the mind keeps winnings, losses and the original stake in separate accounts with different rules. Losing house money does not feel like a loss, and an open loss account makes any bet that could close it look attractive.

items.q: Does the site treat winnings differently from deposits?
items.a: No. The wallet is one balance per coin; a payout is credited to the same number a deposit sits in, and the demo engine works the same way. The game engine reads nothing about previous results when deciding a round.

items.q: How do I avoid betting more after a win?
items.a: Set the stake as a fraction of the balance before the session and keep the fraction when the balance rises, treat break-even as an ordinary number, and use the settings page limits, which lock in a decision made before any win or loss.

items.q: What is takarakuji?
items.a: Japan’s public lottery, issued by prefectures and designated cities under a 1948 law. Proceeds fund local government, and the law caps the prize pool at 50% of sales.

items.q: What was tomikuji?
items.a: The Edo-period temple lottery. Numbered wooden tags were tumbled in a box and pierced with an awl in front of a crowd; the proceeds paid for temple and shrine repairs. The shogunate banned it in 1842.

items.q: What are the odds of winning the Year-end Jumbo?
items.a: About one in 20 million per ticket for first prize. Tickets are issued in units of 20 million, one hundred thousand numbers across two hundred groups, with one first prize per unit.

items.q: How much of a lottery ticket is returned as prizes?
items.a: By law no more than 50% of sales; in practice around 46% in recent years, with roughly 40% going to the issuing governments and the rest to costs.

items.q: How does that compare with the games on this site?
items.a: Bingo returns about 96.5% and every keno table between 98.65% and 99.07%, both computed from engine source. The difference reflects the product: a lottery takes a large share once, a casino game a small share many times.

items.q: Why would a verifier and a server disagree if they use the same hash?
items.a: Because turning a hash into a number between 0 and 1 requires rounding to 53 bits of precision, and rounding once does not always give the same result as rounding several times. A verifier that accumulates bytes in a loop can differ from a server that converts once, in the last bit.

items.q: Does one bit really matter?
items.a: When the number is multiplied by 37 or 52 or a million and rounded down, the last bit can decide which integer results. That is a different pocket, card or item.

items.q: How does the engine avoid it?
items.a: It builds the number from two exactly representable pieces, the first four bytes over 2³² and the next bytes over 2⁵⁶ or 2⁶⁴, and adds them once, matching the single rounding of the server’s integer-to-double conversion. Crash uses exact integer arithmetic and no doubles at all.

items.q: Is the verifier a separate program from the game?
items.a: No. The hash and number functions live in one shared module that both the demo engine and the fairness panel import, so the generator cannot drift from the verifier.

items.q: What does a failed verification mean here?
items.a: That the inputs differ from what the server used, because rounding cannot cause a false failure on this engine. It is the signal the verifier exists to give.

items.q: What is the cursor in a provably fair round?
items.a: A counter inside the round. The message hashed with the server seed is “client seed-nonce-cursor”; cursor 0 gives the first random number the game needs, cursor 1 the second, and so on. A game that needs one number reads cursor 0 only.

items.q: How is the cursor different from the nonce?
items.a: The nonce counts rounds and goes up by one with each bet across every original. The cursor counts draws within one round and restarts at 0 each round. Together with the seed pair they identify every random number the site ever produces.

items.q: How many random numbers does a bingo round use?
items.a: Sixty-three: cursors 0 to 24 lay out the 25 cells of the card and cursors 25 to 62 draw the 38 balls, all without replacement within their pools.

items.q: Does hitting in blackjack change the next card?
items.a: No. Each card is derived from its own cursor in deal order, and the whole list exists once the seed pair and nonce are fixed. Hitting reads the next entry; standing leaves it unread.

items.q: Do all games use the cursor scheme?
items.a: Keno and Crash use hash chains instead: keno hashes a per-ticket random hash and salt ten times, and crash follows the bustabit chain with exact integer arithmetic. The fairness panel verifies each from the strings it shows.

items.q: When did mahjong come to Japan?
items.a: In the first decade of the twentieth century; Natsume Sōseki described it in 1909 after seeing it played in Manchuria. The boom began around 1924, when the first Tokyo parlours opened and Kikuchi Kan championed the game.

items.q: Is mahjong for money legal in Japan?
items.a: No. Article 185 of the Penal Code punishes gambling and exempts only stakes that are “a thing provided for momentary amusement”, which courts have held excludes cash. Small-stake games are widely tolerated but occasionally prosecuted.

items.q: What is a jansō?
items.a: A mahjong parlour, licensed as an amusement business that rents tables and tiles. It is not permitted to host betting; what the players do among themselves is the grey zone.

items.q: What happened in 2020?
items.a: Tokyo’s chief prosecutor was reported to have played mahjong for money with reporters during the state of emergency and resigned. After a citizens’ review panel objected to the initial decision not to charge him, he was fined by summary order in 2021.

items.q: Is there mahjong on this site?
items.a: No. The site offers games whose return is computed from their engine and published; it does not offer a game whose legality depends on the size of the stake.

items.q: What is dust in crypto?
items.a: A balance too small to be worth moving, because the network fee to send it would equal or exceed it. It arises from remainders, rounding, partial fills and occasionally unsolicited transfers.

items.q: Why does the network fee not scale with the amount?
items.a: Because a blockchain charges for the transaction’s size or computation, not its value. Sending one satoshi costs the same as sending one bitcoin in the same transaction shape.

items.q: Why is there a minimum withdrawal on this site?
items.a: Each coin has a minimum and a fee stored in its smallest unit and shown in the withdraw window. A withdrawal below the minimum would spend the network fee and deliver nothing, so the window refuses it before sending.

items.q: Is a balance below the minimum lost?
items.a: No. It remains yours, can be staked, and can be withdrawn once the balance exceeds the minimum.

items.q: Someone sent me a tiny amount I did not ask for. What is it?
items.a: Most often an address-poisoning attempt or an attempt to link your addresses. Do not interact with it and never copy an address from that transaction.

items.q: What does Koban Flip pay?
items.a: ×1.96 per correct call on a fair coin, compounding while you ride. The ladder after n straight wins is floor(1.96ⁿ, 2 decimals), from ×1.96 to ×836.68 at ten wins.

items.q: What is the house edge?
items.a: 2% per flip: a correct call has probability one half and pays 1.96 instead of 2. A ride of n flips has expected return 0.98ⁿ, so the edge per unit of exposure stays 2% however far you ride.

items.q: Are the faces decided as I ride?
items.a: No. One ride is one seed pair and nonce, and flip i is derived from cursor i, so every face is fixed when the first coin is bought. Your calls decide whether a face pays you, never what it shows.

items.q: Can I verify a ride?
items.a: Yes. After the server seed is revealed, all faces of the ride can be recomputed from the seed pair and nonce, including flips after you cashed out.

items.q: What happens at ten wins?
items.a: The pot is credited automatically at ×836.68 of the stake. Ten is the maximum ride length; there is no eleventh cursor.

items.q: What is Fukubukuro on this site?
items.a: A one-draw game: pay the bag price, open it, receive an item worth a fixed multiple of the price. Two bags, Ume with eight items up to ×100 and Matsu with seven items up to ×250.

items.q: What does each bag return?
items.a: Ume 96.6% and Matsu 96.78% of the price on average, computed from the engine’s weight tables as chance × payout summed over the items.

items.q: Does every bag really pay something?
items.a: Yes. The cheapest item is ×0.20 of the price in Ume and ×0.10 in Matsu, so an open never returns zero. Most opens return less than the price: Ume pays at least the price on about 26% of opens, Matsu on about 16%.

items.q: How is the item chosen?
items.a: One number from the round’s hash, scaled to an integer between 0 and 999,999, is compared against the bag’s cumulative weights in millionths. The first item whose cumulative weight exceeds the roll is the result. The reel animation afterwards is display only.

items.q: Which bag is better?
items.a: Neither, by return. Ume is the steadier shape with a ×100 top; Matsu has a harsher floor and a ×250 top. They differ in volatility at nearly the same price.

items.q: How often does the dealer bust in blackjack?
items.a: On this engine’s infinite shoe with the dealer standing on all 17s, about 28% of hands overall: from 35% with a 2 showing up to 42% with a 6, then 26% with a 7, 21% with a ten and 12% with an ace.

items.q: Why is a dealer 6 the best card for the player?
items.a: It is the upcard from which the dealer busts most often, 42.3%, and when the dealer does not bust the most common result is a weak 17. A stiff player hand can stand and let the dealer bust.

items.q: Why is hard 16 the worst hand?
items.a: Hitting it busts 61.5% of the time, and standing on it wins only when the dealer busts. Against a 7 or higher the dealer usually makes a hand, so both options are bad and hitting is merely less bad.

items.q: Are these numbers the same in a real casino?
items.a: Close but not identical. A finite shoe with cards removed shifts every figure slightly, which is what card counting tracks. The infinite shoe here has no removal, so the figures are exact and never change.

items.q: Does knowing the table beat the house?
items.a: No. It explains basic strategy, which on these rules returns about 99.5% according to the engine header. The edge remains with the house.

items.q: How does Casino Hold’em work?
items.a: You post an ante and get two cards; the dealer gets two; a three-card flop is dealt. You call for twice the ante or fold. If you call, the turn and river are dealt and the best five of seven cards on each side are compared.

items.q: What does it mean for the dealer to qualify?
items.a: The dealer needs a pair of fours or better. If the dealer does not qualify there is no showdown: your ante is paid by the bonus table and your call is returned.

items.q: What is the ante bonus?
items.a: On a qualified win, or when the dealer fails to qualify, the ante pays by hand strength: ×101 royal flush, ×21 straight flush, ×11 four of a kind, ×4 full house, ×3 flush, ×2 straight or less, total return. The call pays 1:1 on a qualified win.

items.q: What is the house edge?
items.a: The engine header states about 2.2% of the ante with sound calling. Folding too often raises it, because a fold is a certain loss of the ante.

items.q: Can a folded hand be verified?
items.a: Yes. All nine cards come from one seed pair and nonce in a fixed order; the turn and river are only read if you call, but they can be recomputed after the seed is revealed.

items.q: What is address poisoning?
items.a: A scam in which an attacker generates an address that matches yours or a frequent destination at the beginning and end, then sends a tiny or zero-value transfer so it appears in your history. If you later copy the address from that row, your funds go to the attacker.

items.q: How did someone lose 1,155 bitcoin to it?
items.a: In May 2024 a wallet sent a small test to the right address, then copied the address for the large transfer from a poisoned history row that matched at both ends. The 1,155 WBTC went to the attacker; it was returned about ten days later after a bounty and public tracing, which is rare.

items.q: Can a wrong transfer be reversed?
items.a: No. A confirmed blockchain transaction has no reversal. A stablecoin issuer can sometimes freeze tokens at a known scam address, but that is a property of one issuer’s contract, not of the chain.

items.q: Where should I copy the deposit address on this site?
items.a: From the deposit window, which fetches the address for your account, coin and network from the wallet service and shows a copy button and a QR code for that exact string. If the coin needs a tag, copy it from its own field too.

items.q: What is the simplest defence?
items.a: A rule: never copy a receiving address from a transaction history. Copy it from the place that issued it, check characters in the middle as well as the ends, and use a whitelist where one exists.

items.q: How is a roulette bet represented on this site?
items.a: As a self-describing string: a kind prefix and the numbers it covers, such as n:17, sp:16-17, co:16-17-19-20, dz:2 or ev:red. The engine decodes the string to its pocket set and settles by membership.

items.q: What does each bet pay?
items.a: Total return: straight ×36, split ×18, street ×12, corner ×9, first four ×9, six line ×6, dozen ×3, column ×3, even chances ×2. These match the standard European table.

items.q: Why is every bet the same price?
items.a: Because for every kind the multiplier times the pockets covered equals 36, on a wheel with 37 pockets. Expected return is 36 ÷ 37 = 97.30% and the edge is 2.7% for every bet.

items.q: What stops a malformed bet?
items.a: A validator that requires a known kind, exactly the right number of pockets for that kind, every number in 0…36, and no duplicates. Keys that fail are refused before settlement.

items.q: How is the pocket chosen?
items.a: floor(u × 37), where u comes from cursor 0 of the round’s hash of the committed server seed, your client seed and the round number. One spin settles every key placed on it.

items.q: What is the hot hand fallacy?
items.a: The belief that someone who has just succeeded several times is more likely to succeed next. A 1985 study of basketball shooting found no such effect and named the belief a fallacy; a 2018 paper showed the 1985 test was biased and that the data in fact supported a hot hand in shooting.

items.q: What was wrong with the 1985 test?
items.a: It measured the share of hits following a run of hits within finite sequences and compared it to the player’s overall rate. In a finite sequence that share is expected to be below the true rate even when every trial is independent: about 46% for a fair coin over 100 flips after three heads, and exactly 40.5% over four flips after one head. Against the corrected baseline, the shooters were hot.

items.q: Does the hot hand exist in casino games?
items.a: Not in games of pure chance. The correction concerns skill processes where a person’s state carries between attempts. A die, a wheel or a seeded round has no state to carry, so a streak says nothing about the next result.

items.q: Is a streak on this site random?
items.a: Each round is a hash of the committed server seed, your client seed and the round number, with nothing carried from the previous round. A streak is a run of independent results; it can be recomputed after the seed is revealed but it predicts nothing.

items.q: How is this different from the gambler’s fallacy?
items.a: The gambler’s fallacy expects a reversal after a run; the hot hand expects a continuation. On independent events both are wrong. The 2018 paper adds that measuring runs in short sequences produces a spurious reversal even in perfect randomness, which had been mistaken for evidence.

items.q: What is roulette wheel bias?
items.a: A physical imperfection in a wheel, such as a worn fret or an uneven pocket, that makes some numbers land more often than 1 in 37. Even a small bias is valuable because single-number bets pay 35 to 1: a pocket landing 1 in 30 gives the player a 20% edge on that number.

items.q: Who was Joseph Jagger?
items.a: A British engineer who, in the early 1870s, had clerks record the results of the wheels at Monte Carlo, identified one wheel with nine favoured numbers, and won a reported two million francs betting on them before the casino rearranged its wheels and frets.

items.q: What did the Spanish Supreme Court decide about García-Pelayo?
items.a: In 2004 it ruled that his winnings were legitimate. Recording spins and betting on biased pockets was observation, not fraud; an unmaintained wheel was the casino’s failure. He kept the money.

items.q: Why was Ivey’s edge sorting cheating if wheel bias was not?
items.a: Because of what the player did. García-Pelayo watched and bet on the game as offered. Ivey had the croupier rotate the high cards under a false pretext, so the game he played was not the one the casino thought it was dealing. The English courts called that a sting; the Spanish court called observation legitimate.

items.q: Could wheel bias exist on an online roulette game?
items.a: Not on one derived from a seed. Here the pocket is floor(u × 37) from the committed server seed, the client seed and the round number, which gives every pocket exactly 1 in 37. There is no physical wheel to wear, and any spin can be recomputed after the seed is revealed.

items.q: How many spins does it take to find a bias?
items.a: Thousands of spins of the same wheel. The difference between 1 in 37 and 1 in 30 is about six spins in a thousand, so separating a real bias from noise with confidence takes on the order of several thousand recorded results, which is why both men needed clerks and weeks.

items.q: What was Japan’s first gambling ban?
items.a: A prohibition of sugoroku recorded in the Nihon Shoki for the twelfth month of 689, during the reign of Empress Jitō. It is the earliest gambling law in Japanese written records; the chronicle gives no reason and no penalty.

items.q: What is ban-sugoroku?
items.a: A two-player race game of the backgammon family: fifteen pieces a side moved by two dice around a board of twenty-four points, with the aim of bearing off first. It reached Japan from the continent by the seventh century and died out in the Edo period.

items.q: Is ban-sugoroku the same as e-sugoroku?
items.a: No. E-sugoroku is a later picture race game on a single track, decided entirely by one die, played at New Year. It borrowed the name as the board game faded. Ban-sugoroku involved choices and was the game that was gambled on and banned.

items.q: What did Emperor Shirakawa say about sugoroku?
items.a: The Heike Monogatari attributes to him the remark that three things did not obey him: the waters of the Kamo River, the dice of sugoroku, and the warrior monks of Mount Hiei.

items.q: What is the sugoroku master’s advice in Tsurezuregusa?
items.a: Section 110 records a master saying that one should not play to win but play not to lose: identify the move that would lose fastest, avoid it, and prefer the move that loses slowest. Kenkō applied it to life generally; as bankroll advice it anticipates the modern arithmetic of minimising ruin.

items.q: How are dice generated on this site?
items.a: Each die is a uniform number derived from the committed server seed, your client seed, the round number and a cursor, mapped to 1 through 6. After the server seed is revealed, any roll can be recomputed in your browser.

items.q: What is a hash commitment in a provably fair casino?
items.a: The SHA-256 fingerprint of the house’s secret server seed, shown before play and checked against the seed when it is revealed. It proves the seed was fixed before your bets and that the revealed seed is the one committed to.

items.q: Does a matching hash prove the game was fair?
items.a: It proves the randomness was not altered after commitment and, with a published derivation, that each result follows from the seed pair. It does not prove the seed was chosen randomly, and it says nothing about the house edge, which is a separate published number.

items.q: Can the house pick a server seed that favours it?
items.a: Only if it knows the client seed the server seed will be paired with when it chooses. The defence is to commit the server seed before the client seed is set. On this site a client seed change rotates the pair in the same request, so that ordering cannot be confirmed from the client; the article describes the boundary and the fix that has been proposed.

items.q: How do I check a round myself?
items.a: Rotate the seed to reveal the retired server seed, hash it to confirm it matches the commitment you were shown, then recompute HMAC-SHA256 of the server seed over your client seed, the nonce and the cursor, and pass the result through the game’s published derivation. The seed panel performs the recomputation in your browser.

items.q: Why is the derivation code important?
items.a: Because the hash only pins the seed. Turning the seed into a roll or a card is a function, and unless that function is public a matching hash tells you nothing about whether the result was the one the seed implied. Here the client ships the same derivation the demo uses to generate outcomes.

items.q: Is provably fair better than a licensed RNG audit?
items.a: They answer different questions. An audit certifies a generator’s statistical behaviour over many draws; a commitment lets you check a specific round after the fact. Neither replaces the other, and neither changes the house edge.

items.q: How many balls are drawn in Betkyo Bingo?
items.a: 38 balls from 75, without replacement, on a single 5×5 card with a free centre. Each number on the card is drawn with probability 38/75, about 50.7%.

items.q: How many lines can pay?
items.a: Twelve: five rows, five columns and two diagonals. The payout depends on how many of them complete, in seven tiers from ×1.5 for one line to ×500 for seven or more.

items.q: What are the odds of completing a line?
items.a: About 6.1% for each of the four lines through the free centre, which need four drawn numbers, and about 2.9% for each of the other eight, which need five. On average a card completes about 0.48 lines, and about 37% of cards complete at least one.

items.q: What is the return of Bingo?
items.a: The engine header states about 96.5%, measured over one million simulated rounds, with a 37.1% hit rate. Multiplying the measured line-count distribution by the pay tiers reproduces that figure within rounding.

items.q: Why does the free centre matter so much?
items.a: Four of the twelve lines pass through it and need only four numbers instead of five. On a 38-ball draw that roughly doubles their chance, so the centre lines account for about half of all completed lines.

items.q: Can I verify a Bingo round?
items.a: Yes. The card is cursors 0 to 24 and the balls are cursors 25 to 62 of the round’s seed stream, each an HMAC-SHA256 of the committed server seed over your client seed, the nonce and the cursor. Rebuilding both and counting lines reproduces the payout.

items.q: What is the illusion of control?
items.a: The tendency to expect a better outcome from a chance event than the odds justify because the situation contains cues that normally signal skill, such as choosing, practising or competing. Ellen Langer named and demonstrated it in a 1975 series of experiments.

items.q: Does changing my client seed change my odds?
items.a: No. A different seed produces a different sequence of results drawn from the same distribution, so the return of every game is identical for every seed. There is no lucky seed and no way to search for one, because the server seed in use is known only by its hash.

items.q: Then why can I set a client seed at all?
items.a: So that part of the input to every result is yours and fixed before the server seed is revealed. That is what stops the house from choosing inputs whose results it likes, and it is what lets you recompute any round yourself afterwards. The seed is a verification tool.

items.q: Can I change the seed during a game?
items.a: No. The seed panel refuses a change while a round is open and applies a new seed from the next bet. That rule protects both sides: nobody can swap inputs after seeing where a round is going.

items.q: What does rotating the seed do?
items.a: It retires the current server seed and reveals it, along with the hash it was committed under, and starts a fresh pair at round zero. Hashing the revealed seed and comparing it with the earlier commitment is the check that the house did not change seeds mid-way.

items.q: How much more did people value a ticket they chose?
items.a: In Langer’s lottery study, holders of chosen tickets asked an average of about $8.67 to sell, against about $1.96 for holders of assigned tickets, for tickets with identical odds.

items.q: What is a stablecoin depeg?
items.a: A period when a stablecoin trades on exchanges for meaningfully less (or occasionally more) than the currency it is pegged to. The peg is an issuer’s redemption promise; the depeg is the market doubting it. Fiat-backed coins have recovered from every depeg so far; the largest algorithmic coin, TerraUSD, did not.

items.q: Does a depeg change my casino balance?
items.a: Not the coin balance. Balances here are stored as a count of coin units at the coin’s precision, and bets and withdrawals are made in those units. The fiat line under the balance is that count multiplied by a server-sent price, so it moves with the market; the number of coins does not.

items.q: How low did USDC go in March 2023?
items.a: To about $0.87 on 11 March 2023, after Circle disclosed $3.3 billion of reserves at the failed Silicon Valley Bank. It returned to $1 after US regulators announced on 12 March that all deposits at the bank would be honoured.

items.q: What happened to TerraUSD?
items.a: UST, an algorithmic stablecoin backed by a mint-and-burn mechanism with its sister token LUNA rather than by reserves, lost its peg in the second week of May 2022 and fell below $0.10. LUNA’s price went to effectively zero as the mechanism minted trillions of tokens. Neither recovered.

items.q: Is USDT safe from depegging?
items.a: No stablecoin is guaranteed to hold its market price.
