USDT has traded below a dollar on some exchanges during stress, including briefly around $0.95 in May 2022, and has returned to its peg each time. Its issuer publishes reserve attestations; whether those are sufficient is a judgement each holder makes.

items.q: Should I keep my bankroll in a stablecoin?
items.a: That is a personal decision this article does not make for you. A stablecoin removes day-to-day price swings from the bankroll and makes bet sizes easy to read, at the cost of redemption risk on the issuer. Whatever coin you hold, the game’s odds are the same in every one of them.

items.q: What are the odds of hitting the ×1,000 bucket in Plinko?
items.a: On the 16-row high-risk board, 1 in 65,536 for each edge bucket — 2 in 65,536 for either edge. The ball must bounce the same way on all sixteen rows.

items.q: What is the RTP of Plinko?
items.a: Computed from the engine’s multiplier tables and binomial bucket odds, every board returns between about 98.9% and 99.2% per drop, low, medium and high alike. One board — 9 rows on high risk — sat outside that band on a mirrored cell that was out of place. It was found while this article was being written, reported, and corrected on 4 September 2026; the article says what it was.

items.q: Does high risk have a worse house edge than low risk?
items.a: No. The expected return is about 99% on both. High risk pays below ×1 on about four drops in five and concentrates the value in the rare edge buckets; low risk pays close to ×1 on most drops. The total is the same; the shape is different.

items.q: Do more rows improve the odds?
items.a: They do not change the return, which stays near 99% at every row count. More rows make the edges rarer and the multipliers larger in step, so the ride gets spikier without getting cheaper or dearer.

items.q: Why does the middle bucket pay less than ×1?
items.a: Because it is where the ball most often lands — 19.6% of drops on 16 rows, more on shorter boards — and a game that paid ×1 or better there could not afford its edges. The centre is where the house edge is collected on every Plinko board.

items.q: Can I verify a Plinko drop?
items.a: Each live drop returns the landing bucket and the nonce it drew on, and the seed panel shows the committed server-seed hash and your client seed; the ticket ties a drop to that pair and round. The server-side derivation itself is not in the client code, so verification runs through the ticket and the commitment.

items.q: What is the best bet in Sic Bo?
items.a: Big, Small, Odd and Even, and the two-number combination bet. Each returns 97.22% for a house edge of 2.78%. No other box on the layout is cheaper.

items.q: Why do Big and Small lose on a triple?
items.a: Because that rule is the entire house edge. Big and Small each cover exactly half of the 216 rolls; removing the six triples takes each down to 105 winning rolls, which at ×2 is a 2.78% edge.

items.q: What does a specific triple pay, and what is the edge?
items.a: ×181 total return (180 to 1). It hits on 1 roll in 216, so the return is 83.80% and the edge 16.20%.

items.q: Which Sic Bo bet has the highest house edge?
items.a: On this engine’s Macau-standard paytable, a total of 9 or 12 at ×7 (18.98% edge) and a specific double at ×11 (18.52%). Both hit far more often than a triple and are priced far worse.

items.q: Are the multipliers here the same as a casino’s “pays X to 1”?
items.a: They are the same amounts written as total return. ×2 is 1 to 1; ×31 is 30 to 1; ×181 is 180 to 1. The engine uses total return because that is what the settlement code multiplies the stake by.

items.q: What is edge sorting?
items.a: A technique that exploits a printing asymmetry on the backs of some playing cards. If high cards are turned one way and low cards the other, a player can tell which is coming from the edge before it is dealt. The sorting is done by asking the dealer to rotate certain cards, and it survives only if the shuffle preserves orientation.

items.q: How much did Phil Ivey win by edge sorting?
items.a: About £7.7 million at Crockfords in London in August 2012, which the casino refused to pay, and about $9.6 million at the Borgata in Atlantic City in 2012, which he was later ordered to return.

items.q: Did Phil Ivey cheat?
items.a: In the legal sense, yes. The English High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court all held that edge sorting as he practised it was cheating, and the Supreme Court held that it did not matter whether he personally believed it was honest. A New Jersey federal court found breach of the state’s rules against marked cards rather than fraud, with the same practical result.

items.q: Why is Ivey v Genting Casinos famous among lawyers?
items.a: Because the Supreme Court used it to replace the Ghosh test for dishonesty in English law with an objective test: what did the defendant actually know, and would ordinary decent people regard the conduct as dishonest. That test now applies in criminal cases generally.

items.q: Could edge sorting work on a provably fair card game?
items.a: No. The cards are numbers derived from a committed seed pair and a nonce; there is no physical deck, no back to read, no shuffle to preserve and no dealer to persuade. The next card does not exist until the round derives it.

items.q: What is the RTP of Hanabi?
items.a: Exactly 95.81%, computed from the weights: 66.17% from line wins, 2.87% from scatter pays and 26.77% from the free-spin feature. The engine header’s 96.1% came from a three-million-round simulation and overstated it by about three-tenths of a point. About 33.5% of spins pay something.

items.q: How often do Hanabi free spins trigger?
items.a: On about one base spin in 84. Each of the fifteen cells is a 祭 scatter with probability 2/61, and three or more scatters on a spin start the feature; that binomial count is 1.193%, matching the engine’s measured “≈ 1 in 83”.

items.q: How does the free-spin multiplier work?
items.a: It depends only on which free spin it is: spins 1–2 pay ×1, 3–4 pay ×2, 5–7 pay ×3, and every spin from the eighth onward pays ×5. A plain ten-spin feature averages ×3 per spin; a fully retriggered 22-spin feature averages ×4.1 with its last fifteen spins all at ×5.

items.q: How many free spins can you get?
items.a: Ten to start; each retrigger (three or more scatters inside the feature) adds four, up to a cap of 22.

items.q: What is the maximum win on Hanabi?
items.a: ×2,000 the total bet. The engine settles the round at the smaller of the raw total and the cap, and flags a round that was capped.

items.q: Can I verify a Hanabi spin?
items.a: Yes. Every cell is one weighted draw from the committed server seed, your client seed and the nonce — base spin cursors 0–14, free spin j cursors 15+15j to 29+15j — using the public weight table, so the whole round replays from those three values.

items.q: What is a blockchain confirmation?
items.a: One block added on top of the block containing your transaction. Zero means the network has seen it but not agreed on it; each further block makes reversing it exponentially less likely.

items.q: Why does a casino need several confirmations?
items.a: Because a credited deposit can be wagered and paid out immediately. If the deposit were then reversed by a chain reorganisation, the house would have paid real money against a transaction that no longer exists. The count is the house choosing how small that risk must be.

items.q: Why is it six for Bitcoin?
items.a: From the Bitcoin whitepaper’s calculation: an attacker with 10% of the network has about a 20% chance of reversing a one-confirmation transaction and about 0.02% after six. Six is where the risk becomes negligible for value at rest.

items.q: How many confirmations does Betkyo require?
items.a: It is set per coin on the server and printed on the deposit screen beside the address, because chains settle at different speeds and with different security models. Read the number there; it is the current one.

items.q: My deposit has been waiting for a long time. Is it lost?
items.a: Usually not. Check the transaction in the chain explorer: if confirmations are rising it is on its way; if they are stuck at zero on Bitcoin or Litecoin the fee was likely too low and it is queued; if the explorer cannot find it, check the sending wallet and the network it was sent on.

items.q: What is the house edge on Limbo?
items.a: 1%. The engine’s curve is 0.99/(1−u), and the 0.99 makes the return exactly 99% at every cash-out target you pick — ×1.5 and ×1,000 cost the same.

items.q: What is the house edge on Crash?
items.a: 1%, the same as Limbo. A cash-out is paid only when the bust point is strictly above it, so a target of T hundredths pays 99 ÷ T of the time and returns exactly 99% at every target. (Corrected 2026-09-19; the first version gave 99x/(100x−1).)

items.q: Are Limbo and Crash the same game underneath?
items.a: No. They run different functions for a structural reason: Limbo draws per player from your own seed pair, while Crash draws one number for every player in the round from a pre-committed hash chain.

items.q: Does picking a higher multiplier change the house edge?
items.a: In Limbo, no — the return is flat at 99% across every target, so the choice is purely about variance. In Crash, also no: under the strict settlement every target returns 99%, so there too the choice is purely about variance.

items.q: What is the maximum win?
items.a: ×10,000 in Limbo — the clamp at 1,000,000 hundredths, reached roughly once in 10,101 rounds, and those rounds pay the cap. In Crash the same clamp is the bust point itself, and a cash-out must be strictly below the bust, so the highest target that can pay is ×9,999.99.

items.q: What does blackjack pay at Betkyo?
items.a: 3:2 — a natural returns ×2.5 on the stake. The rule is stated in the engine source alongside S17, double on any first two cards, one split, dealer peek, and no insurance or surrender, at about 99.5% with basic play.

items.q: How much does 6:5 blackjack cost compared with 3:2?
items.a: About 1.4% of every initial stake. A natural arrives on 8/169 of hands (4.73%) on an infinite shoe, and 6:5 pays 0.3 stakes less on each one — nearly three times the entire house edge of a good 3:2 game.

items.q: Can you count cards on Betkyo blackjack?
items.a: No. Cards come from an infinite shoe — each card is an independent draw from all 52, derived from the committed seed pair — so nothing depletes and there is nothing to track.

items.q: Why is there no insurance?
items.a: Insurance is a 2:1 side bet that the dealer has a ten under an ace. With a 4/13 chance of that, it returns 92.3% — the worst bet on a blackjack table. Basic strategy never takes it, so leaving it out costs a correct player nothing.

items.q: Does the dealer stand on soft 17?
items.a: Yes — S17, the player-favourable version. Tables that hit soft 17 give the house roughly an extra fifth of a point.

items.q: What is the house edge on Koban Flip?
items.a: 2% per flip — a fair coin paid at ×1.96 instead of ×2, per KOBAN_WIN_100 = 196 in the engine. But the game is a ladder, so the cost compounds: at ten straight calls the payout is 81.71% of fair value, an 18.3% cost.

items.q: What does a ten-flip streak pay?
items.a: ×836.68, against ×1,024 for a fair coin. The chance of getting there is 1 in 1,024. The ladder is computed as 1.96 to the power of n, floored to two decimals so the display matches what the server settles.

items.q: Why does a 2% edge become 18%?
items.a: Because the game multiplies. Each rung keeps 98% of fair value, and 0.98 raised to the tenth power is 0.817. The percentage never changed; it was applied ten times to a compounding number.

items.q: Can I improve my odds by choosing heads or tails?
items.a: No. Each face is an independent draw from the committed seed pair, and the whole sequence is fixed before your first call. Your decisions change how far you ride, not what the coins show.

items.q: Is cashing out early better than riding?
items.a: It is cheaper in fair-value terms — the shallower the rung, the less the compounding has taken. It is not free money either: every rung still returns 98% of the one below. What early cash-out buys is a smaller price and a smaller swing.

items.q: What is the highest multiplier in Fugu?
items.a: ×3,236,072.40 on screen, for clearing all safe tiles with ten or fifteen mines — C(25,10) × 0.99. It is a property of the formula rather than a paid prize: the guide states that payouts are bounded by the table’s maximum profit.

items.q: Why do ten mines and fifteen mines pay the same?
items.a: Because the full-clear payout is the number of ways to place the mines, C(25, m), times 0.99 — and C(25,10) equals C(25,15). The same symmetry pairs 5 with 20 and 1 with 24.

items.q: Which mine count has the best odds?
items.a: None. The multiplier is 0.99 divided by the probability of reaching each tile, so the expected return of cashing out anywhere is 99% on every board. The mine count changes how the ride feels, not what it costs.

items.q: How is the Fugu multiplier calculated?
items.a: As one exact fraction — the product of (tiles left) over the product of (safe tiles left) across every tile revealed — floored to two decimals, times the table’s return factor (0.99 by default), floored again. The engine computes the products in BigInt because they overflow ordinary numbers.

items.q: What happens if I send crypto on the wrong network?
items.a: If the address format does not match the chain, the sending wallet usually refuses and nothing moves. If it does match — as it does across Ethereum, Polygon and other EVM chains, which share the 0x format — the transfer succeeds on a chain the deposit system is not watching, and it is not credited. Recovery is a manual request and is not guaranteed.

items.q: Is USDT on TRON the same as USDT on Ethereum?
items.a: No. They are separate assets on separate ledgers, pegged to the same dollar. A deposit address is valid on one chain only; the version of USDT you send must be the one that chain carries.

items.q: Why does the deposit screen ask for a network before showing an address?
items.a: Because the address only exists for a specific chain. The wallet asks the server which networks a coin is available on, and issues an address for the one you choose — so that the chain being watched and the chain you send on are the same by construction.

items.q: What is an XRP destination tag?
items.a: A number attached to an XRP transaction that tells a custodian which customer a deposit belongs to. The address routes coins to the custodian; the tag routes them to you. XRP sent without it arrives unattributed and must be matched by hand.

items.q: How can I tell which network an address is for?
items.a: Often from its first characters — T for TRON, r for XRP, 1/3/bc1 for Bitcoin, L/M/ltc1 for Litecoin. The exception is 0x, which Ethereum, Polygon and every other EVM chain share; for those, only the network selector tells you.

items.q: What was the Absolute Poker superuser scandal?
items.a: In 2007, insiders at Absolute Poker used an observer account that could see every player’s hole cards in real time. The account POTRIPPER won a tournament with statistically impossible decisions; a mis-sent hand history containing all hole cards proved it. The regulator found seven linked accounts had cheated over about 40 days; Absolute refunded $1.6 million and paid a $500,000 fine.

items.q: What happened at UltimateBet?
items.a: A larger version of the same breach. Cheating initially admitted for 2006–2007 was eventually traced back to June 2003. The Kahnawake Gaming Commission fined the site $1.5 million, ordered $22 million repaid to players, and named 1994 WSOP champion Russ Hamilton as the main person responsible.

items.q: Was the shuffle rigged?
items.a: No — and that is the point of the story. The deals were fair. The cheats won by seeing opponents’ cards, not by choosing their own. A fairness proof covers the randomness of the draw; it cannot cover the secrecy of information in a player-versus-player game.

items.q: How were the cheats detected?
items.a: By players, statistically. Win rates far outside anything a legitimate edge produces prompted forum analysis; the accidental release of a hand history with hole cards confirmed the mechanism. No audit or regulator caught it first.

items.q: Could a superuser exist in a provably fair house game?
items.a: The attack has nothing to read. In a house game the entire state — your bet, the committed draw, the paytable — is either yours or published. Advance knowledge of the server seed would be an attack on the draw itself, which is what commit-reveal verification exists to expose.

items.q: What is the near-miss effect in gambling?
items.a: The tendency for losses that look close to a win — two of three jackpot symbols, a lottery number one digit off — to feel meaningful and motivate continued play, even though in a game of independent chance they carry no information about future outcomes.

items.q: Does a near miss mean the win is close?
items.a: No. In an independent-draw game the outcome is decided fresh each round. On our Hanabi reels, two scatters landing changes nothing about the third: every cell is a separate weighted draw at the same odds, every round.

items.q: Do slot machines manufacture near misses?
items.a: Some historically did, weighting reel displays so near misses appeared more often than the true odds produce them, and regulators have acted against the practice. Hanabi’s teases occur at exactly the rate independent draws imply — about 7.3% of spins show two scatters, versus 1.2% for the three that trigger free spins — and any spin can be recomputed from its committed seed pair.

items.q: Why does almost winning feel worse and yet make people keep playing?
items.a: That paradox is the core research finding: near misses are rated more unpleasant than full misses while recruiting some of the same reward circuitry as wins. The discomfort and the motivation arrive together, which is what makes the effect worth knowing about by name.

items.q: What do 9/6 and 8/5 mean in video poker?
items.a: The full house and flush payouts per unit bet. 9/6 (×9 and ×6) is the full-pay Jacks or Better table; 8/5 (×8 and ×5) is the common cut. This engine pays 8/5, as VP_PAYTABLE in the source shows; it paid 9/6 until 2026-09-10.

items.q: What is the return of 8/5 Jacks or Better?
items.a: About 97.3% with optimal play, per the engine source (the 9/6 table it replaced ran about 99.5%). The number assumes correct holds on every hand; consistent mistakes lower it by several points. No level of skill takes it above 100%.

items.q: Is video poker a game of skill?
items.a: Partly, and uniquely so in this catalog. The hold decision after the deal changes the return, and optimal play is a learnable ranking of about thirty hand patterns. The ceiling remains the published paytable — skill closes the gap to it, nothing more.

items.q: Can the machine change the draw after I choose my holds?
items.a: No. The entire card sequence is derived from the committed seed pair before your decision — replacements come from a single pre-ordered, without-replacement sequence, and the fairness data lets you recompute it after the round.

items.q: How rare is the royal flush?
items.a: On the order of one in tens of thousands of optimally played hands, per the standard analyses of the game. It pays ×800 here; treating it as the goal rather than the paytable’s top row is the most expensive habit in video poker.

items.q: What is chō-han?
items.a: The classic dice game of Edo-period Japan: a dealer shakes two dice under a cup and players bet on whether the sum is even (chō) or odd (han), paid at even money. It was the signature game of the bakuto gambling clans.

items.q: Is chō-han a fair game?
items.a: In its odds, exactly fair: 18 of the 36 two-dice outcomes are even and 18 are odd, so both sides of an even-money bet have zero expected value. The operators profited by taking an open cut of winning bets — the tera-sen — rather than through the odds.

items.q: Why did the chō-han dealer play half-naked?
items.a: Tradition explains it as live proof of fairness: no sleeves, nothing palmed, the dealer’s skin as the audit. The full-back tattoos it displayed also marked whose table it was. The custom is the pre-cryptographic ancestor of showing your work.

items.q: Does any modern game offer chō-han’s bet?
items.a: Sic bo’s odd and even bets are the same wager on three dice. The difference is the price: both lose on any triple, six outcomes in 216, which gives the house its 2.78% — an edge chō-han’s two-dice version simply did not have.

items.q: Does a higher keno risk level pay better?
items.a: No. Computed from our engine paytable, all forty tables — four risk levels across ten pick counts — return between 98.65% and 99.07% of stake. Higher risk buys larger, rarer payouts at the same average price.

items.q: Does the risk level change my chance of hitting numbers?
items.a: Not at all. Ten balls are drawn from forty regardless, so the chance of hitting a given number of your picks depends only on how many numbers you marked. The risk level only changes what each number of hits pays.

items.q: What are the odds of hitting all ten numbers in keno?
items.a: One in 847,660,528 — that is C(40,10), the number of distinct ten-ball draws from a forty-number board. It is the cell that pays ×1,000 on Low, Medium and High.

items.q: Is it better to pick more numbers or fewer?
items.a: Neither is better on return; each pick count has its own table priced to the same band. More picks means more hits on average — ten picks average two and a half — but the table demands more hits before it pays.

items.q: Can I improve my odds by choosing particular numbers?
items.a: No. Every ten-ball combination is equally likely and the draw has no memory of previous rounds, so no set of numbers is better than another. The draw is committed before you see it and can be verified after the round.

items.q: Who was Ronald Dale Harris?
items.a: A computer engineer employed by the Nevada Gaming Control Board in the early 1990s whose job was to detect software and devices designed to cheat at slot machine play. He used that access to rig machines himself.

items.q: How did Ronald Harris cheat slot machines?
items.a: He modified the software on certain machines so that inserting coins in a specific sequence and number would trigger a large payout. Between 1993 and 1995 he and an accomplice used it to take thousands of dollars from Las Vegas casinos.

items.q: How was he caught?
items.a: Not by a technical control. His accomplice Reid McNeal tried to collect a $100,000 keno jackpot at Bally’s Park Place in Atlantic City; casino executives found his behaviour suspicious and alerted New Jersey gaming investigators. Both were charged on 15 January 1995.

items.q: What happened to him?
items.a: He was sentenced to seven years in prison and released after serving two. He is listed in the Nevada Gaming Control Board’s black book, which bars him from entering licensed casinos in the state.

items.q: Could the keno prediction attack work against a provably fair game?
items.a: Not in the same way. Harris exploited a generator whose output was predictable to someone who knew the algorithm and its state. Under commit-reveal the server seed is committed by hash before the bet and revealed afterward, and your own client seed enters the result — so publishing the algorithm costs nothing, and the outcome cannot be changed once your bet is placed.

items.q: What is the difference between a hot and a cold wallet?
items.a: A hot wallet is online and automated so withdrawals can be paid immediately; a cold wallet keeps keys offline and moves funds only through a human process. Platforms keep a small working balance hot and the bulk cold, because online keys are the ones that get stolen.

items.q: Does proof of reserves mean a platform is solvent?
items.a: No. It shows control of certain assets at a point in time. Solvency depends on assets minus liabilities, and liabilities cannot be proven cryptographically — so reserves without a liabilities attestation prove considerably less than they appear to.

items.q: Is it safer to keep funds on a platform or in my own wallet?
items.a: Your own wallet removes custody risk but adds the risk of losing your own keys, which is a very common way to lose crypto. The practical answer for most people is to keep only what they intend to play with on any platform.

items.q: Why do some withdrawals take longer than others?
items.a: Large withdrawals often require moving funds out of cold storage, which is a deliberate manual step. The delay is a security control rather than a stalling tactic — instant unlimited withdrawals would imply everything is held hot.

items.q: Why do different exchanges show different Bitcoin prices?
items.a: Each runs its own order book with its own buyers and sellers. Arbitrage keeps them close but never identical, and the gaps widen exactly when the market moves fastest.

items.q: Why do oracles use a median instead of an average?
items.a: An average is dragged by outliers, so one broken or manipulated venue moves the result. A median only counts how many sources agree, so an attacker must corrupt a majority rather than a single feed.

items.q: Can a casino manipulate the price a leveraged bet settles on?
items.a: It can if it quotes the price itself, and at high leverage it would only need a fraction of a percent. That is why the meaningful question is whether the settlement reads an independently published feed — one you could look up yourself.

items.q: What stops a stale price from being used to settle?
items.a: A freshness rule. On our desk a tick past its freshness window is not treated as a price at all: it blocks fills and liquidations equally until a live one arrives.

items.q: Can I close my position while the price feed is down?
items.a: No, and neither can the house liquidate you. Both actions require a tick fresh enough to be trusted, and they read it through the same gate, so the pause applies equally to both sides.

items.q: What happens to my position if the feed never comes back?
items.a: After ten minutes dark, it is closed at zero and your full stake is returned. That is the terminating rule — without it, positions would stay open indefinitely with the money frozen.

items.q: I was in profit when the feed died. Do I keep it?
items.a: No. A void settles at exactly zero for everyone, which is what allows the rule to be applied without reference to who was ahead. The same rule protects you when the market moved against you during the outage.

items.q: Do I pay funding for the time the feed was down?
items.a: No. Outage time is credited back to the funding clock on recovery, and a voided position pays no funding and no house share at all.

items.q: Why are there no clocks in casinos?
items.a: Because time awareness is one of the main cues that prompt people to stop. Removing clocks and windows removes the two ordinary ways of noticing how long you have been playing.

items.q: Does online play avoid casino floor psychology?
items.a: No — the same levers exist in different form. There is no closing time, no queue, one tap to play again, and the pace is far faster than any physical table, which multiplies the effect of the house edge.

items.q: Are near-misses deliberately engineered?
items.a: Not necessarily. On a fair game they arise naturally from how paylines are evaluated. What matters is whether reels are weighted to produce them more often than chance would — which is what published paytables and verifiable rounds let you check.

items.q: What is the single most effective countermeasure?
items.a: Deciding your budget and your stopping time before you start, and setting an alarm outside the interface. Decisions made in advance are the only ones the environment cannot influence.

items.q: What is Tairyō’s maximum win?
items.a: ×2,100 of total bet, applied as a hard cap in the engine — so it bounds a round regardless of what the paytable and features would otherwise produce.

items.q: How many paylines does Tairyō have?
items.a: Ten fixed lines on a 5×3 grid. Three are the straight rows and the remainder zig-zag, which is why a screen can look full of a symbol and still pay nothing.

items.q: Why do so many wins pay less than the spin cost?
items.a: Because the low symbols pay ×0.5 of the line bet for three of a kind, and the line bet is a tenth of your total bet. That is normal reel-game design rather than a bad run — a large share of winning spins return less than they cost.

items.q: Do slot features increase the return?
items.a: Usually not. Features redistribute return: they take value out of ordinary spins and concentrate it into rare events. A game with a dramatic feature has a correspondingly quieter base game.

items.q: What is risk of ruin?
items.a: The probability that a losing streak consumes your entire bankroll before you stop playing. It depends far more on your bet size relative to your stack than on the game’s house edge.

items.q: Does a higher RTP mean I am less likely to go broke?
items.a: Only slightly. Return tells you the average cost per bet; survival is governed by variance and bet sizing. A 99% game bet at a fifth of your bankroll is far more dangerous than a 97% game bet at a hundredth.

items.q: Is a big bet or many small bets safer?
items.a: Neither is safe against a negative edge — they fail differently. Small bets survive longer but give the edge more chances to work; large bets shorten exposure but invite ruin from an ordinary losing run.

items.q: Can bet sizing beat the house edge?
items.a: No. No staking system changes the expected value of a negative-edge bet. Sizing changes how long your money lasts and how violent the swings are, which is worth managing — but it is not an edge.

items.q: Is pachinko legal gambling in Japan?
items.a: Pachinko is legal precisely because it is not classified as gambling. Players win balls, exchange them for prizes in the parlour, and sell those prizes for cash at a legally separate business — so no single entity pays money for a game of chance.

items.q: What is the three-shop system?
items.a: The chain of three formally unrelated parties — parlour, off-premises prize buyer and wholesaler — that lets pachinko winnings become cash without any one of them both running the game and paying out money.

items.q: How big is the pachinko industry?
items.a: Historically one of the largest leisure sectors in Japan, with peak figures in the tens of trillions of yen — though those are usually total money staked rather than operator revenue. The industry has contracted substantially since the 1990s.

items.q: Why does Japan allow it if gambling is banned?
items.a: Because each individual step is lawful and the parties are separate entities. Machine payouts are nonetheless regulated by the state, which is the same oversight a gambling regulator applies.

items.q: Does yakuza really come from a card game?
items.a: It is the standard and most widely accepted account: 8-9-3 is the worthless hand in Oicho-Kabu, read ya-ku-za in the older numeral forms. Like most etymologies of this age it rests on tradition rather than a dated document.

items.q: Why does 8-9-3 score zero?
items.a: Oicho-Kabu counts only the last digit of a total. Eight plus nine plus three is twenty, which ends in zero — the lowest score the game has.

items.q: Is Oicho-Kabu the same game as baccarat?
items.a: Not the same game, but the same counting: score modulo ten with nine as the target. Both descend from a broad family of nine-counting card games rather than one from the other.

items.q: What are kabufuda cards?
items.a: A Japanese deck numbered one to ten with four of each card, used for Oicho-Kabu and related games — a cousin of the hanafuda flower deck rather than a Western suited pack.

items.q: How unlikely is 26 blacks in a row?
items.a: On a European wheel it is (18/37)^26, roughly 1 in 137 million for any given run of 26 spins. Across every wheel that has ever spun, however, a streak like it was close to inevitable somewhere.

items.q: Was the Monte Carlo wheel rigged?
items.a: There is no evidence of it, and none is needed. The run is improbable for one particular sequence and unremarkable across the number of spins the world’s casinos have collectively made.

items.q: Was betting on red the mistake?
items.a: Not in itself — red carried the same slightly negative expectation as anything else on that wheel. The mistake was raising the stake each time on the belief that red was overdue, which turns a small disadvantage into a total loss when the streak continues.

items.q: Do streaks make the next spin more likely to correct?
items.a: No. Each spin is independent, and long-run balance comes from later results diluting the imbalance rather than from any correction of it. The past spins are never repaid.

items.q: What move liquidates a ×1000 position?
items.a: A move of 0.1% against you. The liquidation distance is always 1 ÷ leverage, so ×1000 busts on a tenth of a percent — about $64 on a $64,000 Bitcoin.

items.q: Can I lose more than I put in?
items.a: No. Realized loss is floored at the stake in the settlement code itself, so a gap or a crash through your bust price still costs you exactly what you opened with and nothing more.

items.q: Does higher leverage improve my chances?
items.a: No. It changes the size of the outcome and the distance the price may travel first. The probability of being right about direction is unchanged, which is why extreme leverage shortens the average life of a position rather than improving it.

items.q: Why did my position close when the price barely moved?
items.a: Two possibilities: the move was larger relative to your leverage than it looked in dollar terms, or funding consumed the margin. Past the first hour, funding is charged on notional, and at high leverage the notional is large enough to exhaust a stake on its own.

items.q: What is the Kelly criterion?
items.a: A formula giving the fraction of a bankroll to stake to maximise long-run growth: f* = (bp − q) ÷ b, where b is the odds received, p the chance of winning and q its complement.

items.q: What does Kelly say about casino games?
items.a: To bet nothing. Every house game has a negative expectation by design, and Kelly returns zero or a negative fraction whenever the expectation is not positive.

items.q: Can Kelly betting beat the house edge?
items.a: No. No staking method changes the expected value of a bet. Kelly optimises how to exploit an edge you already have; it cannot manufacture one.

items.q: Why do professionals bet fractional Kelly?
items.a: Because the full formula assumes you know your edge precisely, and nobody does. Betting a half or a quarter of Kelly sacrifices some growth for a large reduction in the damage done by overestimating the edge.

items.q: What does the house take on a losing trade?
items.a: Nothing. The share applies only to positive net profit. Losing closes and liquidations pay no fee, and a liquidation costs exactly the stake with nothing added.

items.q: What is the fee at ×1000?
items.a: 10% of net profit — the ceiling of the curve. At the other end, ×1 pays 2%. Every rung in between is interpolated, so there is no boundary where the rate jumps.

items.q: Is the rate locked when I open?
items.a: It follows the leverage you opened at, and leverage is fixed for the life of a position, so the rate a position pays is settled the moment you enter it.

items.q: Why scale by leverage and not by size or hold time?
items.a: Hold time is already priced by funding, and size is left out to keep the number explainable. Leverage is the one input the player picks deliberately and can see, which is what makes showing the exact rate possible at all.

items.q: Do I need to know cryptography to verify a round?
items.a: No. The manual path needs nothing beyond pasting strings into any SHA-256/HMAC calculator. Understanding why it works takes a paragraph; performing it takes a minute.

items.q: Why do I have to rotate my seed to verify?
items.a: Because the server seed must stay secret while it is still producing rounds — revealing it early would let a player compute future results. Rotation ends the seed’s life, which is exactly what makes it safe to reveal and audit.

items.q: Could the house generate a lucky seed for itself?
items.a: The commitment blocks the useful version of that: the seed is fixed before your bets and mixed with a client seed you control. The house would need to predict your seed, your bet, and your timing — at which point it is no longer running a casino but a mind-reading act.

items.q: Is provably fair the same as being licensed or audited?
items.a: No — they answer different questions. Audits and licenses are institutional trust; provably fair is mathematical trust in each individual result. We publish the math and our full paytables so the two claims are never confused.

items.q: What is the single most important habit?
items.a: Deciding the session budget before the session, in an amount you can lose entirely without consequence — and treating its loss as the session ending, not as a situation to fix.

items.q: How does self-exclusion work on Betkyo?
items.a: Contact support and specify a duration between six months and five years. The exclusion cannot be undone within that period, and opening a new account during it is prohibited — the permanence is the protection.

items.q: Is there a “safe” amount of gambling?
items.a: There is no universal number; the honest test is functional: budgeted entertainment money, no chasing, no concealment, no borrowed stakes, and stopping feels available. When any of those fails, the amount is beside the point.

items.q: Is it smarter to cash out early or climb in Pagoda?
items.a: Neither, by expected value — every exit returns exactly 99% of stake in the long run. Climbing buys a smaller chance of a larger payout at the same price; the right floor is a preference about variance, not a strategy.

items.q: Could the trap move after I start picking?
items.a: No. All nine trap positions derive from the seed pair committed before the round, each floor from its own cursor. Rotate your seed and you can recompute the full tower — including floors above where you stopped.

items.q: Why does HARD pay ×506.88 and not ×512?
items.a: ×512 is the fair value of nine doubled floors (2⁹); 506.88 is 512 × 0.99 — the house edge applied once to the whole ladder. That single application is what keeps the expected return identical at every cash-out point.

items.q: Are omikuji considered gambling in Japan?
items.a: No — at a shrine you pay a small offering and always receive a fortune; nothing is staked and nothing is won. It is divination with the mechanics of a lottery, which is exactly why the format adapts so naturally to one.

items.q: What should you do with a bad fortune (凶)?
items.a: Custom says tie it to the pine or the rack provided at the shrine — the misfortune “waits” there instead of following you home. Keeping a good fortune in your wallet is equally traditional.

items.q: Did Japan really choose a shōgun by lottery?
items.a: Yes — in 1428, the sixth Ashikaga shōgun was selected by lots drawn before Hachiman from four candidate brothers. Ashikaga Yoshinori is remembered, not always fondly, as the kuji-biki shōgun.

items.q: Is card counting illegal?
items.a: No — using your memory and arithmetic at a table is legal. Casinos, as private venues in most jurisdictions, respond by refusing service: backing players off, restricting bets, or banning them. Devices that count for you are a different, criminal matter in many places.

items.q: How big was the MIT team’s edge really?
items.a: On the order of 1–2% over the house at favorable counts — comparable in size to the edge the house normally holds. The fortune came from disciplined bet-sizing on that sliver across thousands of hands, not from dramatic single nights.

items.q: Does card counting work online?
items.a: Against RNG blackjack that reshuffles every round — including ours — no; there is no depleting shoe to track. Live-dealer games with deep shoe penetration can in principle be counted, which is why they shuffle early and often.

items.q: Was the film “21” accurate?
items.a: Loosely. The team, the spotter/big-player structure and the bannings are real; characters, dramatic arcs and much of the plot are inventions layered on Mezrich’s already-dramatized book. The reliable parts are the boring ones: training, checkouts, bankroll rules.

items.q: Can a drand member cheat?
items.a: A single member — or any group below the threshold — cannot predict, withhold meaningfully, or bias the output: partial signatures reveal nothing alone, and the combined value is the unique valid signature for the round. Cheating requires a colluding threshold of independent institutions, which is the explicit trust assumption.

items.q: If BLS signatures are deterministic, how is the output random?
items.a: Deterministic means uniquely determined by the key and the round — not knowable in advance. To anyone without a threshold of key shares, the upcoming signature is computationally indistinguishable from random until it is published. Determinism is what removes choice; secrecy is what preserves surprise.

items.q: Why doesn’t Betkyo just use drand for everything?
items.a: Cadence and binding. Solo games need a result per click, priced per player, with the player’s own seed in the mix — that is commit-reveal’s territory. Beacon-style randomness earns its keep where one draw must serve everyone at once, and the fairness page states the scheme per game rather than pretending one tool fits all.

items.q: What is the oldest known randomizer?
items.a: Astragali — the four-sided ankle bones of hoofed animals — are among the oldest, used across the ancient world for games and divination long before cubical dice standardized the shape of chance.

items.q: Why can’t a computer produce true randomness?
items.a: A deterministic machine given the same state always produces the same output. Computers therefore either harvest entropy from the physical world (noise, timing, hardware sensors) or stretch a small true-random seed into a long pseudo-random sequence — which is exactly what makes committed seeds auditable.

items.q: Is pseudo-randomness good enough for gambling?
items.a: Cryptographic pseudo-randomness is — the sequences are computationally indistinguishable from true randomness, and in a commit-reveal scheme the determinism becomes a feature: it is what lets you recompute and verify a past round exactly.

items.q: Does Nintendo still sell hanafuda?
items.a: Yes. Nintendo still manufactures hanafuda in Japan, including premium lines and Mario-themed decks — a quiet acknowledgment of where the company came from.

items.q: Is koi-koi a gambling game?
items.a: Koi-koi is the most popular hanafuda game today: players capture cards to form scoring combinations (yaku) and choose whether to bank points or press on — that press-your-luck call is the “koi-koi”. Like any card game it can be played for stakes, but the game itself is a folk game taught to children.

items.q: Where does the word “yakuza” come from?
items.a: From oicho-kabu: the hand 8-9-3 (ya-ku-sa) totals 20, which counts as zero — the most worthless hand in the game. Gamblers adopted the term for themselves; the etymology is the standard account given in histories of the Japanese underworld.

items.q: Did the 1913 Monte Carlo streak really happen?
items.a: Yes — the run of 26 blacks on August 18, 1913 is the textbook case, cited across probability literature for over a century. The wheel was examined and found normal; the players’ reasoning was the only broken mechanism in the room.

items.q: Is the gambler’s fallacy the same as the hot-hand fallacy?
items.a: They are mirror images: gambler’s fallacy expects a streak to reverse (“red is due”), hot-hand expects it to continue (“I’m rolling”). Both project memory onto independent events.

items.q: Does provably fair make the odds better?
items.a: No — it makes the odds honest. Verification proves results were fixed at commitment and mapped through the published rules; the house edge in those rules is disclosed separately on each game’s odds panel.

items.q: What actually helps if I keep chasing losses?
items.a: Pre-committed limits, breaks, and — if it recurs — self-exclusion and professional support. BeGambleAware offers free, confidential help; Betkyo support can enforce a self-exclusion period on request, as described on our responsible gaming page.

items.q: Which scheme is the “most fair”?
items.a: They answer different threats. Commit-reveal gives each player a private, free proof; beacons give everyone one public proof; VRFs give machines a checkable proof; certified hardware gives regulators an audited process. A house is judged by whether the scheme it claims is real and whether its odds are published — not by which scheme it picked.

items.q: Can these schemes be combined?
items.a: Yes, and good systems do: a house can commit a mapping, feed it a beacon pulse, and let players check both — commitment for the house’s half, threshold trust for the raw number. Composition covers assumptions a single scheme leaves open.

items.q: Does provably fair mean the house edge is low?
items.a: No. Verification and pricing are independent. A game can be provably fair with any edge — which is exactly why the edge must be published separately, and why we do.

items.q: If the house always has an edge, is playing irrational?
items.a: It is irrational as an investment and rational as entertainment — the same way a concert ticket is a bad investment and a fine evening. The test is whether you are paying a price you know, with money budgeted for entertainment, for an experience you enjoy.

items.q: Why do casinos hide RTP if the edge is defensible?
items.a: Because an illegible price extracts more than a legible one — players who cannot compare games cannot shop. The practice persists because it works commercially; it is criticized because it works by degrading the player’s understanding.

items.q: Does Betkyo profit from player losses?
items.a: Yes — over the long run, by the published edge of each game, like every house. What we refuse is profiting from misunderstanding: the edge is printed, results are verifiable, and the interface never celebrates a loss.

items.q: Why is the same USDT cheaper on one network than another?
items.a: Because the token rides different ledgers with different pricing: a congested computation-metered chain charges more per transfer than one with allowance-based pricing. The token’s value is identical; the postage differs.

items.q: What happens if I deposit on the wrong network?
items.a: It depends on the mistake, and some are unrecoverable — which is why the wallet makes you pick the network explicitly. If it happens, contact support with the transaction details before attempting anything else.

items.q: Why does my deposit need confirmations?
items.a: A transaction becomes trustworthy as blocks pile on top of it; each block makes reversal exponentially harder. Waiting for a few confirmations is the ledger’s settlement process, the same for every service on the chain.

items.q: Does Betkyo add its own margin to network fees?
items.a: The fee you see in the wallet before confirming is the cost applied to your withdrawal — shown in advance, per our terms, so you can always decline. Network conditions, not the house, drive its size.

items.q: Is chinchiro the same game as cee-lo?
items.a: They are cousins. Cee-lo (四五六, “4-5-6”) is the Chinese-American branch of the same family: identical instant-win 4·5·6 and point mechanic, but usually played without a bowl and with different banking rules.

items.q: What does ションベン (shonben) mean?
items.a: Literally “piss” — a die that escapes the bowl. Street rules treat it as a fouled throw; harsher tables treat it as an instant loss. Digital chinchiro has no bowl physics, so the term survives only as flavor.

items.q: Was chinchiro legal in Japan?
items.a: Private dice gambling has been prohibited in Japan since the Meiji era, which is exactly why chinchiro lived in back rooms and fiction rather than casinos. The game itself — dice, bowl, rules — is simply a folk game; it is the wagering that the law regulated.

items.q: What is the best possible payout in Betkyo’s chinchiro?
items.a: A total return of ×6 on your stake: rolling pinzoro (1·1·1) against a dealer point. Dealer hifumi pays ×3 without you rolling at all.

items.q: Was the $40 million real?
items.a: The figure is widely reported and consistent across tellings, but it was never audited — casinos do not publish player balances. What is certain from many witnesses: the stakes were the largest of that era, and the fortune, whatever its exact size, was entirely gone by late 1995.

items.q: Was Karas cheating during The Run?
items.a: No such claim attaches to The Run itself — the 2013 card-marking conviction came nearly two decades later, at small stakes. The Run is remembered precisely because it appears to have been legitimate variance at unprecedented size.

items.q: Could The Run happen on a provably-fair site?
items.a: The verification changes nothing about variance — a fair game still swings, and commit-reveal only proves each result was honest. What a transparent house adds is that a streak like Karas’s could be audited round by round, and that the published edge tells you in advance how the story ends if the player never stops.

items.q: Can I bet after the boosts are revealed?
items.a: No. Betting locks when the deal starts, and the boost stamp is the first thing that happens after the lock. The order is enforced in the round flow, not just the UI.

items.q: Do boosts apply to ANDAR/BAHAR main bets?
items.a: No — boosts multiply side-bet (bucket) wins only. The main bets pay a fixed ×1.9 (ANDAR) and ×2.0 (BAHAR).

items.q: Why does ANDAR pay less than BAHAR?
items.a: ANDAR receives the first raced card, so it wins the race 51.50% of the time against BAHAR’s 48.50%. The lower payout compensates for the higher win rate; with these payouts the house edge is 2.15% on ANDAR and 3.00% on BAHAR.

items.q: What is the biggest possible win in Andar Bahar here?
items.a: A total return of ×3,750 per unit staked: the 46–49 bucket (base ×750) landing while it carries a ×5 boost. The bucket itself hits in about 1 of every 1,041 races.
